items.body: YONGSAN, Republic of Korea — The Republic of Korea-U.S. Combined Forces Command hosted the 2026 ROK-U.S. Combined Warfighting Forum Sept. 16 at the Defense Convention Center in Yongsan, Seoul, bringing together approximately 200 senior military leaders and experts to discuss combined warfighting approaches and capability development for the Korean Peninsula. The forum focused on Combined Joint All-Domain Operations, CFC’s theater-level operational concept for integrating capabilities across the land, maritime, air, space, cyberspace and electromagnetic spectrum domains. U.S. Army Gen. Xavier T. Brunson, commander of CFC, delivered the keynote address during the opening ceremony. CFC Deputy Commander Gen. Kim Sung-min also delivered opening remarks, emphasizing the importance of developing a common combined, joint and all-domain mindset and maintaining interconnected communications. The forum brought together Gen. Jin Yong-sung, chairman of the Republic of Korea Joint Chiefs of Staff; former CFC commanders and deputy commanders; senior leaders from the combined component commands; and military experts from industry, academia and research institutions. CJADO expands traditional approaches to land, maritime and air operations by incorporating space, cyberspace and the electromagnetic spectrum. The concept is designed to integrate operations and capabilities across domains through advanced command-and-control systems to address the evolving security environment and changing character of warfare. Retired ROK Army Lt. Gen. Chun In-bum, former commander of the ROK Army Special Warfare Command, moderated the first session, while U.S. Army Lt. Gen. Joseph E. Hilbert, CFC chief of staff, moderated the second. The first session, titled “CJADO Concept and Capability Development,” examined the U.S. military’s Joint All-Domain Operations concept and its application within the combined ROK-U.S. environment. U.S. Army Lt. Col. Casey L. Miller, U.S. Army Futures Command, presented an overview of JADO, including its definition and key concepts, and discussed considerations for developing CJADO as an extension of JADO into a combined operating environment. The discussion also examined how CJADO should evolve to address the unique operational environment of the Korean Peninsula and identified key enabling capabilities, including command and control, information and data sharing, and artificial intelligence. Panelists included U.S. Army Maj. Gen. William A. Ryan, CFC assistant chief of staff for operations; Col. Matthew Skaggs, CFC deputy director for intelligence; ROK Army Maj. Gen. Choi Chang-soo, director of combat development, ROK Joint Chiefs of Staff; Professor Han Sang-geun, Joint Forces Military University; and Kim Jung-soo, managing director of Anduril Korea and a retired ROK Air Force brigadier general. The second session, titled “Challenges and Solutions for Implementing CJADO,” focused on the challenges associated with implementing the concept and the evolving role of commanders in an all-domain operating environment. Ahn Byung-oh, a researcher with the Defense AI Policy Research Division at the Korea Institute for Defense Analyses, presented on the subject before former CFC commanders and a former deputy commander joined a panel discussion. Retired U.S. Army Gen. Robert B. Abrams and retired U.S. Army Gen. Paul J. LaCamera, both former CFC commanders, and retired ROK Army Gen. Ahn Byung-suk, former CFC deputy commander, shared their experiences and perspectives on the competencies required to operate in an environment where large volumes of information and diverse warfighting capabilities must be integrated across multiple domains. The perspectives and recommendations exchanged during the forum will inform CFC’s continued development of the CJADO concept and the combined capabilities required to implement it on the Korean Peninsula. CFC will continue to strengthen combined warfighting capabilities and interoperability to maintain a strong combined defense posture and safeguard peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula. The continued integration of ROK and U.S. capabilities across domains reinforces the cohesion and interoperability of the ROK-U.S. military alliance and supports the combined force’s ability to respond to an evolving security environment.

items.title: NASA Boss: Race to Moon Has National Security Stakes
items.author: Greg Hadley
items.summary: NASA is pushing hard to get astronauts back to the moon by 2028—and the urgency is driven in no small part by the national security implications of doing so before China does, Administrator Jared Isaacman said Sept. 15. The post NASA Boss: Race to Moon Has National Security Stakes appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. —NASA is pushing hard to get astronauts back to the moon by 2028—and the urgency is driven in no small part by the national security implications of doing so before China does, Administrator Jared Isaacman said Sept. 15.

Speaking at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference, Isaacman said collaboration between his civilian agency and the Pentagon, which are distinct from each other, is important and radically different from the the People’s Republic of China’s lunar ambitions, which does not clearly distinguish between military and civilian operations.

“Success in this endeavor will be measured in months, not years,” Isaacman said. “Our allies and adversaries are watching. So is every nation deciding whose technology to buy, whose standards to adopt, whose security relationships to deepen, and whose vision of the future to follow.”

The Chinese government is targeting 2030 for a manned lunar mission. The U.S. is currently targeting 2028, but that timeline has fluctuated and is considered ambitious. That two-year advantage, Isaacman acknowledged, could easily vanish.

“They have an achievable two-launch architecture to put their Taikonauts on the moon,” Isaacman said, referring to plans to launch the crew and their lander separately. “They have demonstrated reusability with their rockets. They have the expertise, and history has shown they could even be early—and we could easily be late.”

There are immediate, obvious advantages to being first. The moon’s south pole is both rich in resources and a harsh environment that could act as a proving ground for future Mars missions.

But there are “limited parking spots,” as Isaacman put it. “It creates an urgency, and we must, because the Chinese are going to the exact same locations,” he said.

American prestige and dependability in the eyes of the world is also at stake, he suggested.

“If we come up short, if we fail in this regard, and the Chinese are able to get there … It causes all our allies to question whose security guarantees again do you trust? Whose technology should I follow? Whose standards should I adhere to?” Isaacman said. “These are real implications.”

The U.S.’s victory in the first space race against the Soviet Union made an impact on national security, he argued: “I’d love to think July 20, 1969, sent a message to all our adversaries around the world: ‘I wonder what else America is capable of achieving, and maybe I should think twice before I encroach on their interests.’ And I absolutely believe the inverse is true, and it invites encroachment if you fail.”

The Soviet Union never made it to the moon, but Isaacman made clear he doesn’t expect the PRC to falter.

“China will accomplish what the Soviets never could,” he said.

More X-Planes?

The PRC doesn’t draw a line between its military and civil space efforts, Isaacman noted, so any moon base the Chinese establish could have national security implications.

NASA has always been dedicated to the peaceful exploration of space, having been established explicitly outside of the Defense Department. But working together is hardly unusual, Isaacman said, noting that NASA and the Pentagon have long shared knowledge and resources, and must continue to do so in the years to come.

“We should absolutely be collaborating, especially as we think about the cislunar environment, on areas that benefit our civil ambitions, our scientific breakthroughs that we are pursuing, but also enhance our national security footprint farther out into space,” he said.

As an example, he cited both organizations’ work on nuclear power in space. If NASA and the Pentagon pursue separate projects, the resources each can devote to it will be cut, reducing the odds of success, Isaacman said.

NASA and the Air Force have collaborated in the past on aeronautics research, and Isaacman said the agency is re-devoting itself to that field after years of neglect. As things stand, he said, NASA has devoted its aeronautics budget to helping industry squeeze more efficiency out of mature engine technologies.

“That is not what your NASA’s aeronautics budget should go to,” Isaacman said. “Very unapologetically, we are absolutely pivoting away from that.”

Instead, Isaacman wants the agency to focus on “game-changing” technologies, building he said. Right now, NASA has just one experimental “X-plane,” the X-59 , meant to explore supersonic flight without loud booms.

“That will change,” Isaacman said, promising more X-planes are in the works.

At AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference, CAE takes Air & Space Forces Magazine behind the scenes of Valiant Shield 26, a Pacific exercise in June and July of 2026 focused on integrated air and missile defense and the defense of Guam. Matthew Martins explains how CAE used live, virtual, and constructive (LVC) simulation to generate complex threats and enable Army, Navy, and Air Force teams to train together on operational command-and-control networks.

items.title: Soldiers and civilians carry the legacy of 9/11
items.author: SSG William Parsons
items.summary: Soldiers, first responders and community members gathered in Tempe, Arizona, Sept. 10–13, 2026, to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. Through an enlistment ceremony, memorial observances and the Tunnel to Towers 5K run, participants honored those lost and reflected on a legacy of military and civilian service.
items.body: TEMPE, Ariz. – It has been 25 years since the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, and for several days Tempe Beach Park transformed into a memorial honoring those killed. From Sept. 10-13, day and night, crowds gathered amidst the sprawling field of stars and stripes to remember what was lost that day. In attendance were politicians, law enforcement officers, first responders, veterans, survivors, and various guest speakers. Yet it was a small gathering of young men and women who marched before the crowd that made the event feel different. Here, these future Soldiers raised their right hands and swore an oath of enlistment to defend the United States. Capt. Simon Lee, executive officer of the Tempe Recruiting Company, Phoenix Recruiting Battalion, said his knowledge of 9/11 came from history books and the experiences imparted by those who lived through it. “September 11th is something that obviously is ingrained into me because that is something I grew up my whole life with,” Lee said. As an officer in charge of the future Soldiers, Lee said that he wanted the memorial to bring meaning to the swearing-in ceremony. “It's not just them signing a piece of paper, but an actual commitment to a life of service.” For other Soldiers present, a lifetime of service was something they were very familiar with. “September 11th, that's why I joined the Army,” said Command Sgt. Maj. Sean Stoddard of the 4th Battalion, 361st Infantry Regiment. An Army Reserve Soldier who deployed to Afghanistan and Iraq, Stoddard also served for 15 years in the Mesa Police Department. It was this confluence of military and civilian service that Stoddard hoped his unit would bring to the memorial. “I love to see our battalion getting together, unified with the community, one team, one fight,” Stoddard explained. “We're celebrating the Soldiers that are here, the firefighters, first responders, law enforcement.” Stoddard recalled how he nearly lost his life while on duty as a police officer, when his patrol car was struck by another vehicle – leaving him with a traumatic brain injury, amnesia, and temporary blindness. During his recovery, he had to rediscover many aspects of his life all over again. “I had to relearn 9/11,” he said. Once on his feet again, Stoddard went back to doing what mattered to him: selfless service. “We are served by the previous generations,” said Stoddard. “We are currently served. We will be served in the future, and there's blessing and joy in service.” Many at the memorial did not wear a uniform while serving others. For Stella and John Herold, volunteer event directors for the Tunnel to Towers Foundation, service has become an integral part of their lives. Responsible for overseeing the 9/11 memorial event in Tempe as well as a 5K run, the couple have a strong personal connection with what happened on that fateful day. “I lost my older brother, Gary, in the South Tower,” said John. Gary died while leading his coworkers to the stairwell during the attacks. This year, Kyle Carman, interim fire chief for the Tempe Fire Medical Rescue Department, carried Gary’s flag with him during the run. “We’re here to do something good. This is our country,” explained John. “And this country will never be taken away from us because of that spirit.” The Healing Field at Tempe Beach Park was set up by the Tunnel to Towers Foundation and contains American flags representing all of the fallen. Families and strangers alike walked through the rows of flags to read the names. Stella had a message for those worried about approaching the field. “Touch those flags, read those names,” she said. “It's breathtaking to see, to stand back and watch all the candles going into the field, all the people, and they're reading names, stories.” Standing before the vast sight, Lee reflected on its impact. “When you actually see the representation of those numbers here on the field with family members who have been affected, it's extremely powerful just knowing how deeply rooted this is into our culture.” By bringing the future Soldiers to this memorial, their service became intertwined with the history of 9/11. Lee said the Soldiers who join today come from all different backgrounds but arrive at the same place for the same reason. “The biggest thing with joining the military is it's obviously something that you don't do just for your own personal benefit,” he explained. “You do it for others.”

items.title: AMC deputy commander emphasizes long-range airpower, mobility integration at AFA 2026
items.author: 1st Lt. Kevin Powers
items.summary: Maj. Gen. Gerald Donohue, deputy commander of Air Mobility Command, joined military and defense industry leaders to address service members, partners and journalists on the evolving demands of long-range airpower during the Air and Space Forces Association’s Air, Space and Cyber Conference, Sept. 15, 2026.
items.body:
Maj. Gen. Gerald Donohue, deputy commander of Air Mobility Command, joined military and defense industry leaders to address service members, partners and journalists on the evolving demands of long-range airpower during the Air and Space Forces Association’s Air, Space and Cyber Conference, Sept. 15, 2026.

Donohue joined Maj. Gen. Ty W. Neuman, commander of Eighth Air Force and the Joint-Global Strike Operations Center, and Jamie Burgess, Vice President and General Manager of Mobility, Surveillance and Bombers at Boeing, for a panel discussing long-range airpower with a focus on Operation Midnight Hammer and Operation Epic Fury.

During the discussion, Donohue highlighted the essential role of tanker and strategic airlift platforms in bridging global distances to generate decisive combat power without requiring forward-prepositioned strike forces, emphasizing the historic performance of mobility Airmen who did not miss a single Air Refueling Control Time during recent high-tempo operations.

“When we think about the way we've been able to project power, whether it be from the continental United States or from other locations where it's forward-postured, Air Mobility Command, the Air National Guard and Air Force Reserve Command—who are undergoing the biggest mobilization in a generation or two—have been committed all in and extraordinarily effective,” Donohue said. “A tanker fleet that is largely defined by 70-year-old aircraft, sustained by extraordinary maintainers and supported by a global en route structure to ensure it is ready to meet the challenge, has delivered.”

Echoing the strategic synergy required for global strike, Neuman emphasized that bombers and tankers operate as an inseparable system of systems when executing deep-penetration strikes.

“In the near term, we have to have a combat bomber force that has the long-range strike capability, supported by our AMC brethren, to get to the fight with the appropriate capabilities to inflict the necessary pain and suffering on the adversary,” said Neuman.

Addressing the realities of modernizing a legacy refueling fleet, Donohue outlined how AMC is pursuing recapitalization and upgrades across three primary categories: connectivity, survivability and viability.

“Largely today, some of our forces still operate the way they did 20 years ago, and they don’t have the connectivity that you have when you get on your flights to head home,” Donohue explained. “Epic Fury and Midnight Hammer underscored the importance that connectivity plays—not only to our own survivability, but more importantly, to the success of the Joint Force.”

To illustrate the scale of joint warfighting interoperability, Donohue highlighted the massive refueling and airlift footprint required to launch and recover global strike packages.

“When we talk about Midnight Hammer, most public attention rightly focuses on the extraordinary stealth bomber aircrews who executed the mission. What most Americans don’t fully understand is the dozens and dozens of tankers and airlift assets that were necessary to make that happen,” Donohue stated.

Looking ahead, Donohue cautioned that while the acquisition of the KC-46A Pegasus continues to deliver critical capability, the Air Force must remain clear-eyed about the timelines required to modernize the mobility enterprise.

“The last KC-135 pilot has not been born,” said Donohue. “That is just a statement of fact when we consider the time it takes to modernize and so we will have to sustain our legacy platform as well as our newest platforms and ensure that the Joint Force is supported by being able to execute the mission.”

Donohue concluded by expressing his deep gratitude for the Airmen across Active, Guard and Reserve components who make global reach a reality every day.

“The nation should be proud of its mobility Airmen,” Donohue concluded. “Whether it’s in our global AOC, the 618th Air Operations Center, our contingency response, or our global air mobility support structure…we have set the theater. And then ultimately, to the tanker aircrews who made every one of the [Air Refueling Control Times] to ensure that [Neuman’s] team can deliver the desired effects, we should all be proud of what that force is able to accomplish.”

items.title: AETC Boss Maps Path for New T-7 to Reach Initial Operational Capability
items.author: Matthew Cox
items.summary: The Air Force is targeting August 2027 for its new T-7A Red Hawk trainer jet to reach its initial operational capability. To get there, the head of Air and Education Training has three milestones he needs to see the program hit. The post AETC Boss Maps Path for New T-7 to Reach Initial Operational Capability appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. —The Air Force is targeting August 2027 for its new T-7A Red Hawk trainer jet to reach its initial operational capability. To get there, the head of Air and Education Training has three milestones he needs to see the program hit.

The 99th Flying Training Squadron at Joint Base San Antonio-Randolph, Texas, recently received its third T-7, a next-generation trainer designed to be representative of the fourth- and fifth-generation fighters that pilots will fly in the Combat Air Force. To reach IOC, the command must have a total of 14 T-7s, said Maj. Gen. Clark Quinn.

“We are expecting at least two, and most likely three more this year at Randolph,” Quinn told reporters Sept. 15 at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference. “And if I fast forward to January 2027, we’ll really start getting about one a month.”

At the same time, the command must have at least 14 of its initial training instructors certified on the new aircraft, Quinn added. AETC announced its first two qualified instructor pilots in June.

There’s precious little wiggle room in the schedule, the AETC commander acknowledged.

“Production has to be on time because I have to spin up all those instructor pilots to be ready,” Quinn said. “The 14 aircraft can’t show up in July; I need them to show up on the schedule that they’re on.”

In addition to the 14 aircraft and 14 instructor pilots, Quinn also said the T-7’s “capabilities need to be opened up through developmental tests to allow me to fly the profiles that I need to train pilots.”

The Air Force Operational Test and Evaluation Center and the 412th Test Wing are f lying a combined developmental and operational testing campaign; developmental testing ensures the aircraft meets its capability requirements.

“As of right now, we are on track for August to make all of those goals, assuming those three things happen,” Quinn said.

Replacing the T-6?

The Red Hawk was originally developed to replace the aging T-38 Talon which have been in service since the 1960s. But at last year’s Air, Space & Cyber conference , AETC officials said they had also begun exploring whether they can shift some training duties to the T-7 from the T-6 Texan II, used for undergraduate pilot training.

At this year’s conference, Quinn was noncommittal.

“There has been no decision made on if we would go to a single aircraft pipeline,” Quinn said, adding that there are both “pros and cons” to that path.

“The pro being, if you have to have an entire additional weapon system that you are maintaining with logistics, supply, it’s very expensive,” Quinn said. “It requires more instructor pilots, requires more maintainers. … There is a con to a single aircraft pipeline, which is if something ever happens to that aircraft that would prevent it from flying for an extended period of time, I really don’t have a backup plan to that.”

For now, Quinn said he needs to “get the aircraft routinely flying in the hands of my instructor pilots to determine if we are confident that somebody that has never flown a military aircraft can get in that thing on day one and not only be safe but actually learn.”

“We just have not flown it enough at Randolph with my instructor pilots yet,” he added. “So, until I get the confidence that my instructors think that we can do this, that opens the door to then make that decision.”

The Air Force announced in May that it has approved T-7 to move into low-rate production and awarded Boeing a $219 million contract to start building the first 14 production jets. The program has seen its share of challenges. The service awarded Boeing a $9.2 billion contract in 2018 for the T-7, and the company and service touted the use of digital design techniques as a groundbreaking step that would streamline the Red Hawk’s development, production, and sustainment.

But design, testing, and production problems emerged that caused repeated delays to the T-7’s schedule. The Air Force’s original plan called for buying the first operational T-7s in 2023, before ejection seat and flight control software problems caused that deadline to slide, first to 2024, then 2025.

items.title: Weight they carry: Fort McCoy firefighters honor those lost on 9/11
items.author: Scott Sturkol
items.summary: Twenty-five years after the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, the memory of the emergency responders who ran toward danger that morning remains deeply connected to the work of firefighters who continue to answer calls for help today.
items.body:
Twenty-five years after the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, the memory of the emergency responders who ran toward danger that morning remains deeply connected to the work of firefighters who continue to answer calls for help today.

That connection was especially visible Sept. 11, 2026, at Fort McCoy as Firefighter/Emergency Medical Technician Brandon Perron and fellow Fort McCoy Directorate of Emergency Services Fire Department firefighters Stephen Darling and Luke Erickson participated in the installation’s annual 9/11 Memorial Run and Stair Climb.

Nearly 100 Soldiers, veterans, military retirees, Fort McCoy employees and others participated in the 2026 event, which included a 2.975-mile run/1.34-mile walk followed by a stair climb inside one of Fort McCoy’s four-story barracks buildings. The stair climb is designed as a physical remembrance of the thousands of emergency responders who climbed the stairs of the World Trade Center towers after the attacks.

For Perron, the event has become a deeply personal tradition.

Perron, a Sparta, Wisconsin, native, was in fifth grade when the attacks occurred. In previous years, he explained that watching the events unfold helped inspire his decision to become a firefighter.

“I kind of knew at that point that firefighting was something that I wanted to do,” Perron said in a 2025 Fort McCoy interview.

In 2024 and 2025, Perron completed the Fort McCoy event wearing his full firefighter turnout gear and carrying more than 100 pounds of equipment. In 2025, it marked his second consecutive year completing the event in that manner.

The equipment was not simply extra weight.

Perron carried a high-rise pack and a New York hook as a way of symbolically representing the equipment firefighters carried into the World Trade Center. The firefighters responding to the towers had to take breathing-air bottles, hose and other tools up hundreds of feet of stairs because elevators were unavailable or unsafe.

“It’s to honor the 343 firefighters who perished on 9/11 and those who have perished since because of cancer related issues,” Perron said in 2024. “But it’s also just in the totality of the circumstances that everybody who has either fought in the wars following and lost their lives or the civilians who lost their lives. Police officers … everybody who was involved with 9/11 … just to honor and respect them for what they’ve gone through and what their families are going through currently.”

That remembrance extends far beyond the 343 members of the Fire Department of the City of New York who died that day.

Remembering New York's emergency responders

The attacks on the World Trade Center produced what was one of the largest emergency mobilizations in New York City history.

Firefighters, police officers and emergency medical personnel from throughout the New York area responded to the World Trade Center. They faced an almost unimaginable rescue mission as thousands of civilians attempted to escape the burning towers.

After American Airlines Flight 11 struck the North Tower at 8:46 a.m., and United Airlines Flight 175 struck the South Tower at 9:03 a.m., emergency responders moved toward the buildings while civilians moved away.

Firefighters entered the towers to search for and evacuate civilians. Police officers helped direct people toward safety. Emergency medical personnel treated injured people and established medical operations around the disaster site.

Then the towers collapsed, and 343 FDNY firefighters died on 9/11. There were 23 members of the New York City Police Department died, and 37 members of the Port Authority Police Department died.

In all, 411 emergency workers were killed in the attacks.

Those numbers represent individuals — firefighters, police officers, paramedics, emergency medical technicians and other responders — who reported for duty that morning and answered a call unlike anything they had encountered before.

For the FDNY, the loss was particularly devastating. Fire companies from throughout New York City responded to the World Trade Center. Firefighters climbed upward into the towers carrying the equipment necessary to perform rescues and fight fires. Many never came back down.

Their sacrifice also continued long after Sept. 11, 2001. Thousands of first responders and survivors have experienced illnesses associated with exposure to the toxic dust and debris at the World Trade Center site. Numerous emergency responders have died in the years since from illnesses attributed to their service at Ground Zero.

That continuing loss is part of what Perron has sought to recognize through his participation at Fort McCoy.

A legacy carried forward

That idea — answering the call when others need help — is familiar to the Fort McCoy Fire Department.

The installation’s firefighters protect a nearly 60,000-acre Army training center, but their emergency-response mission also reaches beyond the installation through mutual-aid agreements with surrounding communities.

Fort McCoy firefighters have provided assistance during structure fires, vehicle accidents, water rescues, wildland fires and other emergencies throughout the region. The department's capabilities have also expanded well beyond traditional structural firefighting.

For nearly 15 years, Fort McCoy has maintained a specialized scuba dive team, providing a technical-rescue capability that is uncommon among Army fire departments. The team conducts surface and underwater rescue and recovery operations and provides mutual-aid support to surrounding communities.

Its specialized equipment includes dry suits, full-face masks and wireless underwater communications systems. Firefighters regularly train for open-water and ice-rescue operations at Fort McCoy's lakes.

That training has translated into real-world response.

In January 2019, Fort McCoy firefighters responded to an emergency at Perch Lake in Sparta after children fell through the ice, including one who went beneath the surface. Seven firefighters on duty responded, while three additional firefighters came from home to support the dive team.

The department also regularly trains in technical rescue, including rope rescue and high- and low-angle operations.

Fort McCoy maintains aircraft-rescue firefighting capabilities near the Sparta-Fort McCoy Airport, giving the department specialized capabilities for aviation emergencies.

Service beyond the gates

One of the clearest examples of the department’s commitment to surrounding communities came during the catastrophic flooding of August 2018.

After portions of the region received as much as 12 inches of rain, flash flooding overwhelmed communities near Fort McCoy.

Fort McCoy firefighters were called to provide mutual aid.

They responded with personnel, boats and vehicles to Sparta, Melvina and Leon. The department deployed eight firefighters, three boats and four support vehicles during the flood-rescue operations.

Firefighters used boats to reach residents trapped by rapidly rising water. In one case, crews helped evacuate a senior citizen and her granddaughter from a home as floodwater rushed through the area. In another, firefighters used boats to reach residents who were unable to leave their homes.

Overall, emergency responders working in Leon, Sparta and Melvina helped save 57 people and 27 pets.

Among the Fort McCoy firefighters participating in those flood-rescue operations was Luke Erickson, who joined Perron and Darling for the 2026 9/11 Memorial Run and Stair Climb.

That connection gives the 2026 event an especially meaningful dimension. Erickson has not only trained to respond to emergencies. He has answered the call during an actual disaster, helping people in danger in communities surrounding Fort McCoy.

Equipment built for the mission

The Fort McCoy Fire Department’s equipment reflects the breadth of its emergency-response mission.

During the 2018 floods, firefighters used boats capable of navigating dangerous floodwaters. The department's skimmer boat is a 20-foot, water-jet-propelled boat capable of operating in shallow water.

The department’s dive equipment allows firefighters to conduct underwater searches in conditions ranging from open water to beneath the ice.

During annual ice-diving training, divers use dry suits and full-face masks while remaining connected by tether and communications lines to firefighters on the surface. This allows the team to practice lost-diver and underwater-search scenarios under controlled conditions.

The department also maintains specialized wildland firefighting equipment. In March 2026, Fort McCoy firefighters responded to a wildland fire in the installation's North Impact Area after training munitions ignited dry vegetation. Nine firefighters deployed with four brush trucks and a wildland utility terrain vehicle.

The brush trucks carried water tanks, pumps, hoses and wildland tools, while the UTV provided a smaller, highly maneuverable firefighting platform for areas larger vehicles could not easily reach.

Firefighters established a firebreak using back-burn operations and contained the fire in less than two hours without requiring outside mutual aid.

Earlier in 2026, Fort McCoy firefighters also provided mutual-aid assistance during a fire in Tomah.

Each response is different. The equipment changes. The circumstances change. The people needing help change. But the mission remains the same.

Remembering through service

For Darling, Erickson and Perron, participating in the 2026 event placed them among the many Fort McCoy Soldiers, veterans, employees and community members who came together to remember Sept. 11.

For these three firefighters, however, the morning carried an additional meaning. They are members of the profession that was so profoundly affected that morning 25 years ago.

They wear protective equipment.

They train for emergencies that can change in seconds.

They climb toward danger while others are trying to get away.

And they understand the weight of the tools they carry.

Perron’s participation in previous years made that symbolism especially visible. Carrying more than 100 pounds of firefighter equipment up the stairs was a physical representation of what firefighters faced inside the World Trade Center.

In 2026, he was joined by Darling and Erickson.

Together, the three Fort McCoy firefighters honored the fallen by doing something firefighters have done for generations: showing up, carrying the equipment, climbing the stairs and answering the call.

The Fort McCoy 9/11 Memorial Run and Stair Climb cannot recreate what happened in New York City on Sept. 11, 2001.

It does something more important.

It remembers.

It remembers the civilians who never made it home.

It remembers the firefighters, police officers, paramedics and other emergency responders who ran toward danger.

It remembers the families who lost loved ones.

And it reminds those who continue to serve that the legacy of those responders lives not only in memorials and ceremonies, but in the everyday actions of people willing to help others in their greatest moments of need.

Twenty-five years later, three Fort McCoy firefighters carried that legacy up the stairs. And with every step, they carried the memory of those who never came back down.

Fort McCoy’s motto beginning in 2026 is “Training the Total Force and Shaping the Future since 1909.” The installation’s mission: “Fort McCoy strengthens Total Force Readiness by serving as a training center, Mobilization Force Generation Installation, and Strategic Support Area enabling warfighter lethality to deploy, fight, and win our nation’s wars.”

And Fort McCoy’s vision is, “To be the premier training center supporting the most capable, combat-ready, and lethal armed forces.”

Located in the heart of the upper Midwest, Fort McCoy is the only U.S. Army installation in Wisconsin. The installation has provided support and facilities for the field and classroom training of more than 100,000 military personnel from all services nearly every year since 1984.

Learn more about Fort McCoy online athttps://home.army.mil/mccoy, on Facebook by searching “ftmccoy,” on Flickr at https://www.flickr.com/photos/fortmccoywi, and on X (formerly Twitter) by searching “usagmccoy.” Also try downloading the My Army Post app to your smartphone and set “Fort McCoy” or another installation as your preferred base. Fort McCoy is also part of Army’s Installation Management Command where “We Are The Army’s Home.”

items.body: On Sept. 15, under the direction of U.S. Southern Command (SOUTHCOM), Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere (JTF-WHEM) forces successfully interdicted a floating refueling station supporting illicit at-sea drug trafficking operations in the Eastern Pacific. Intelligence confirmed the vessel's involvement with the Los Choneros violent narco-terrorist organization. Individuals removed from the vessel will be transferred to Ecuadorian authorities. After clearing the vessel and disembarking the crew, U.S. forces sank it. JTF-WHEM continues to conduct precise and professional operations to dismantle the logistical networks fueling narco-trafficking in the Western Hemisphere. "We are exerting unrelenting pressure on these narco-terrorists and hurting them where it counts: dismantling their intricate networks, disrupting their sophisticated logistics, and dealing a blow to their finances. This is what total systemic friction looks like," said the commander of U.S. Southern Command, Marine Gen. Francis L. Donovan.

items.title: B-52 Engine, Radar Upgrades Hit New Milestones
items.author: Steve Losey
items.summary: The Air Force’s program to re-engine the B-52H Stratofortress has moved from its technology maturation and risk reduction phase to engineering and manufacturing development, marking a new milestone in the sweeping overhaul of the Cold War-era bomber, a top official said Sept. 15. The post B-52 Engine, Radar Upgrades Hit New Milestones appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. —The Air Force’s program to re-engine the B-52H Stratofortress has moved from its technology maturation and risk reduction phase to engineering and manufacturing development, marking a new milestone in the sweeping overhaul of the Cold War-era bomber, a top official said Sept. 15.

William Bailey, who is performing the duties of assistant secretary of the Air Force for acquisition, technology and logistics, told reporters at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference that the B-52 ’s Commercial Engine Replacement Program entered the EMD phase in June.

The B-52’s Radar Modernization Program , which will replace the bomber’s legacy analog AN/APQ-166 radar with an active electronically scanned array AN/APQ-188 radar, also entered low-rate initial production in August, Bailey said.

The EMD phase of a program’s acquisition process is where prototypes are developed, built, and tested to make sure they meet all the necessary requirements before the system enters production. It follows a Milestone B declaration, which is considered the point where a program formally starts.

The engine and radar replacement programs are some of the most significant upgrades in the B-52’s long history, intended to keep the 1960s-era bombers flying until at least the 2050s. When those and other modernizations are in place, the bomber will be so significantly changed the Air Force plans to redesignate it the B-52J.

Under the reengining program, the B-52’s original TF33 engines, made by Pratt & Whitney, will be replaced with Rolls-Royce-made F130 engines.

The 1960s-era TF33 engines are approaching the end of their service lives and frequently break, Air Force officials have repeatedly said. Many spare parts for the engines are no longer made, forcing the service to find new sources for those parts, make them in-house, or even “cannibalize” them from retired or otherwise non-flying B-52s.

The new Rolls-Royce engines are intended to solve those problems. Not only will they be new, with modernized subsystems like hydraulic pumps and generators that won’t need as much work, they will be derived from commercially used engines, making it much easier to find spare parts.

In an announcement released soon after Bailey’s remarks, the Air Force said the engine program’s Milestone B decision was made June 1 and established the program’s first official acquisition program baseline. CERP’s total acquisition cost was set at $20.2 billion, including the cost of research, development, test and evaluation, procurement, and military construction. The Air Force said that $2.6 billion of that $20.2 billion cost has been spent since 2018.

“The baseline reflects a realistic, data-driven service cost position that accounts for the complexity of integrating new systems on a 70-year-old airframe,” the Air Force announcement states.

The Air Force also said it has “made significant progress” to reduce the risks facing the program. Wind tunnel tests early on found inlet airflow distortion, the statement said. To fix that problem, engineers redesigned the nacelle and inlet, validated the solution through testing, and finished the critical design review with Boeing—which originally made the B-52 and is leading its modernization today—and Rolls-Royce in May 2026.

Two B-52s have been earmarked as test aircraft for the new engines and radar and recently underwent depot maintenance. They are currently flying operational missions, the Air Force said but will travel to Boeing’s facility in San Antonio, Texas, in the next few months to receive both new engines and the new radar.

The first B-52 that was used to test the new radar crashed at Edwards Air Force Base, Calif., in June, killing all eight Airmen and contractors aboard. The Air Force later said another B-52 was being modified with a new radar as a second test aircraft, but that the service always planned to have two radar test aircraft.

Bailey said at the conference that he is still awaiting more information from crash investigators, and that a final decision on how to proceed with the second radar test bomber is still in the works.

“We’re looking at that test aircraft, we had two aircraft from [the Radar Modernization Program], and what do we need to do with that second aircraft as part of the rest of that test program,” Bailey said.

The Milestone C decision authorizing low-rate initial production for the B-52’s new radar was made Aug. 21, the Air Force announcement said. The service awarded a $603 million contract to Raytheon Technologies to start building the radars, and a $163 million contract to Boeing for aircraft integration kits, with the first lot consisting of four kits. The program plans five production lots to deliver 74 kits total.

The Air Force said in its statement that the B-52 modernization program still includes work on survivable nuclear command-and-control communications, including terminals that would operate at extremely high frequencies, and conventional beyond-line-of-sight capabilities like hybrid satellite communication systems.

Part of the the engine program’s Milestone B evaluations included reviewing the B-52’s structural integrity, which remains strong, the Air Force said. The B-52’s airframe can safely support new engines, increased electrical power generation and decades more of flying operations, the Air Force announcement states.

Bailey praised the teams working on the engine and radar upgrades for getting the programs to these critical points.

“That’s the byproduct of a lot of great modeling, a lot of great ground testing, understanding what the engine is going to need to do,” Bailey said. “That [radar milestone] is also after a lot of great work getting through the integration challenges of getting that radar, and all the support equipment that radar needs, integrated into that aircraft.”

But with only 75 B-52s in the Air Force’s fleet and the Stratofortress in heavy demand for the conflict with Iran and deployments elsewhere around the globe , balancing the fleet’s testing, maintenance, and operational needs is a challenge, Bailey said.

“There’s a really great team between [Air Force Global Strike Command], operators of the aircraft, the depot out at Tinker [Air Force Base], the program office, and Edwards Air Force Base, ” Bailey said. “Those communities have to come together in a balance, because a jet needs to be downrange, but a jet also needs to be sustained.”

items.title: Budget Impasse Will Stall 10 Percent of Space Force Programs, Officials Warn
items.author: Courtney Albon
items.summary: The Space Force estimates about 10 percent of its programs will be impacted under a continuing resolution for the coming fiscal year, according to Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess. The post Budget Impasse Will Stall 10 Percent of Space Force Programs, Officials Warn appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. —The Space Force estimates about 10 percent of its programs will be impacted under a continuing resolution for the coming fiscal year, according to Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess.

Earlier this month, Congres s passed a continuing resolution funding the government through Dec. 11 , and while the move ensures there will be no government shutdown when the new fiscal year begins Oct. 1, it also prolonged a major budget impasse that lawmakers and defense experts don’t expect to be resolved anytime soon. The stopgap measure funds government agencies, including the Defense Department, at prior-year levels, which means that any new programs are on hold until a full-year appropriation is passed.

Speaking with reporters at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference, Schiess said the Space Force can move forward with about 90 percent of its programs but the rest will be in limbo under the CR.

“We’re thankful that we have a CR going into Oct. 1, but I would really be more thankful if we have a budget,” he said. “It’s going to slow us down, and the threat is not slowing down. So, I just urge our congressional colleagues and our folks to get after getting us the budget.”

The Pentagon is no stranger to operating within the constraints of continuing resolutions. DOD has started the fiscal year without new appropriations in 38 of the last 50 years , and Schiess noted that the Space Force has functioned under CR conditions for more than half of its seven-year existence.

But this year is different, because of the scale of the increase the service requested for fiscal 2027 —$71.1 billion compared to around $31.6 billion last year. The budget proposal would put the service on a path to double in size over the next few years from around 10,000 Guardians to 20,000. Without it, those expansion efforts will stall, officials warned.

“We need to be able to move forward with the acquisition process so we can build and take possession of the systems we need to help provide that to the mission,” Chief Master Sergeant of the Space Force John Bentevigna said Sept. 15.

The CR also comes as the Space Force is working to speed up its acquisition processes, making plans to start fielding large fleets of targeting, tracking, and communication satellites in the coming years. Erich Hernandez-Baquero, the new assistant secretary of the Air Force for space acquisition and integration, told reporters the budget impasse will likely slow the “ramp up” the service started in fiscal ‘26.

“This CR is definitely going to put the brakes on that for a time period,” he said in a Sept. 15 roundtable. “It really does pace us at a time where we really need to go faster.”

Reconciliation

Further complicating the Defense Department’s fiscal ‘27 budget outlook is its reliance on a $350 billion reconciliation package to supplement a $1.15 trillion base request. That separate reconciliation request is stalled in Congress for now, and it’s unclear what the path is to fund the programs included in that package.

The reconciliation proposal includes a number of Pentagon priorities, including $17 billion for Golden Dome, and about $12 billion in funding for Space Force programs, like Space-Based Air Moving Target Indication and the Space Data Network.

Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said that the funding included in the reconciliation proposal is key to kick-starting Space Force growth in the coming years.

“Those things won’t happen without a budget,” he said. “I think we have general support for Congress on those things. We’ve had great discussions with them. But we can’t continue those things without the budget request in both base and reconciliation.”

items.title: Department of War, state agencies airlift support to Kauai after Hurricane Lowell
items.author: Capt. Casey Sturdivan
items.summary: In the aftermath of Hurricane Lowell, Governor Josh Green requested military assistance to transport specialized utility vehicles from Hawaii Island to Kauai to assist with continued widespread power outages.
items.body:
JOINT BASE PEARL HARBOR-HICKAM, Hawaii — In the aftermath of Hurricane Lowell, Governor Josh Green requested military assistance to transport specialized utility vehicles from Hawaii Island to Kauai to assist with continued widespread power outages. This airlift was an integrated effort, coordinated between the U.S. Pacific Command, U.S. Air Force, Hawaii National Guard and Hawaii Emergency Management Agency, executed by the 15th Wing on Sept. 12 – 13, 2026.

Power outages began Monday as Hurricane Lowell approached Kauai. By 6:40 a.m. Tuesday, approximately 36,000 residents across the island were without electricity.

"I simply decided that we had to do everything possible to shorten the time to recovery, and partnering with the military and utilizing our National Guard on the ground has been a major addition to our state and county efforts," said Governor Green.

Utility trucks originally relocated from California to Hawaii Island in the wake of Tropical Cyclone Lala were loaded onto two Hickam-based C-17 Globemaster IIIs for transport. The equipment was flown from Hilo to Lihue to be repurposed on Kauai to restore essential services.

On the ground, Department of War Emergency Preparedness Liaison Officers and Hawaii National Guard members received the equipment. The airlift augmented support from the 74 members of the National Guard who are currently providing Kauai ground support in the wake of the storm.

“I feel the State of Hawaii Department of Defense is extremely fortunate to be located in such proximity to U.S. Pacific Command and the Pacific Air Forces which enables a rapid response and unity of effort in times of crisis," said Hawaii Adjutant General, Maj. Gen. Stephen Logan.

Transport of the utility vehicles will aid the approximate 6,800 residents that were still without power as of Sunday evening.

“We are committed to continuing support for our community members without power in whatever way we can,” said Col. Kyle Clinton, 15th Wing commander. “Supporting those that support us in times of emergency is why many of us chose to serve.”

These consolidated partnerships across Department of War and state agencies enable near real-time synergistic response capabilities to natural disasters across the Hawaiian Islands.

Imagery and video of this airlift and additional military support efforts in the wake of Hurricane Lowell are available on the official DVIDS feature page: https://www.dvidshub.net/feature/Hurricane-Lowell

items.title: More Fighters Deploy to Middle East Amid Readiness Concerns
items.author: Chris Gordon
items.summary: A fresh National Guard squadron of F-16 Fighting Falcon jets is rotating into the Middle East, seven months into the U.S. conflict with Iran. The high operational tempo of fighter units is prompting the Air Force to address concerns about extended deployments in the Middle East and their implications for readiness. The post More Fighters Deploy to Middle East Amid Readiness Concerns appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine</
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.— A fresh National Guard squadron of F-16 Fighting Falcon jets is rotating into the Middle East, seven months into the U.S. conflict with Iran.

Additional F-16s from the Guard are deploying to U.S. Central Command, people familiar with the matter told Air & Space Forces Magazine, likely to replace one or more units in theater. The fresh jets heading to the Middle East include F-16s from the Oklahoma Air National Guard, sources said. The Air Force began rotating combat units in the Middle East earlier this month, with F-35s from the Wisconsin Air National Guard replaced a unit from the Vermont ANG, and F-16s from the Ohio National Guard replacing a squadron based in Europe.

Fighter units’ high operating tempo has wreaked havoc on the Air Force’s intended rotational model over the past year, prompting growing concerns about extended deployments in the Middle East and their long-term implications for readiness. U.S. military officials acknowledge the concerns, which were also flagged in a new Pentagon Inspector General report . AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies estimates 25 squadrons—around 324 fighters—have deployed so far for Operation Epic Fury.

Those deploying include warplanes based in Europe, where the U.S. maintains three permanently assigned fighter wings flying F-35 Lightning II s and F-15E Strike Eagle s at RAF Lakenheath, U.K., and F-16 Fighting Falcons at Spangdahlem Air Base, Germany, and Aviano Air Base, Italy.

The commander of U.S. Air Forces in Europe-Air Forces Africa, Lt. Gen. Jason T. Hinds, told reporters on Sept. 15 that he and his senior enlisted advisor, Chief Master Sergeant Joshua J. Wiener, have raised their concerns about the high ops tempo with the Pentagon; so has U.S. European Command boss Air Force Gen. Alexus G. Grynkewich, they said.

“One of the concerns the chief and I share all the time is the wellbeing of our men and their family members,” Hinds said during a roundtable at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference. “That affects readiness, it affects retention, and that’s on the front of our minds. And I’ll tell you: It’s on the front of Gen. Grynkewich’s mind. He’s helped us tell that story back into the Pentagon. Same with the Vice Chief and the Chief of Staff of the Air Force—and I’m grateful for them. We’ve given them some specific examples.”

Aviano’s 555th Fighter Squadron returned home earlier this month, having been deployed since November 2025. In July, the 480th Fighter Squadron at Spangdahlem returned to the Middle East just weeks after coming home when tensions with Iran increased.

Many of those units have been deployed to the Middle East routinely over the past several years, ever since Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel ignited conflict in the region. Those conflicts have extended from Iran in the east, Iraq and Syria to the north, and Yemen to the south. Operation Rough Rider , the U.S. campaign against the Houthi rebels in Yemen in spring 2025, preceded Operation Midnight Hammer in June.

Hinds said the Air Force has been keeping up with the maintenance requirements for his deployed units.

“I’ve seen really high readiness rates of the airplanes,” he said. “They’re flying their tails off, which means the Airmen that are flying and fixing them are getting a lot of reps and sets of doing their core jobs.”

Yet keeping up the intense rate of deployments could have an impact on future retention, Hinds said. “I’ve seen some of our Airmen where they’ve been deployed to CENTCOM,” he added. “They come back home, and then shortly there shortly thereafter they deploy to CENTCOM again or elsewhere.

“There’s a lot to think about, how you do that effectively to keep them motivated still,” he added. “They’ve been through a lot, things that I’ve never experienced. I’ve never experienced a ballistic missile blowing up 50 feet from me, right?”

items.summary: More than 1,200 New York Army National Guard Soldiers and 275 military vehicles assigned to the 369th Division Sustainment Brigade maneuvered across five states by highway and cargo aircraft during annual training 2026, officially designated as Operation Sustain Thunder.
items.body:
CAMP SMITH TRAINING SITE, Cortlandt Manor, N.Y. — More than 1,200 New York Army National Guard Soldiers and 275 military vehicles assigned to the 369th Division Sustainment Brigade maneuvered across five states by highway and cargo aircraft during annual training 2026, officially designated as Operation Sustain Thunder.

The two-week exercise, which moved troops and heavy trucks from home armories across New York to Fort A.P. Hill, Virginia, validated the brigade's readiness to mobilize on short notice and keep the Troy-based 42nd Infantry "Rainbow" Division supplied during combat.

The multi-state movement combined long-distance road convoys with heavy strategic airlifts conducted in partnership with the New York Air National Guard's 105th Airlift Wing, based at Stewart Air National Guard Base in Newburgh. Air crews flew six C-17 Globemaster III missions to transport heavy trucks and support teams.

“It was an incredibly proud moment seeing 18 months of planning culminate in moving 1,200 Soldiers and over 275 vehicles from New York down to Fort A.P. Hill,” said Lt. Col. David Myones, who directed airfield operations. “Working with C-17 cargo planes shows why teaming up with the Air Force is so vital.”

Myones added that air integration gives combat commanders maximum operational flexibility.

“In high-intensity combat, our brigade has to deliver fuel, clean drinking water, ammunition, and replacement parts across land, sea, and air,” Myones noted.

The joint airlifts provided critical hands-on experience for flight planners preparing military vehicles to meet strict Air Force flight regulations.

“Moving Army trucks by air takes far more planning than just driving to the runway,” said Warrant Officer 1 Robert Bassett, a brigade mobility warrant officer. “Every vehicle must meet strict size and weight limits.”

Bassett added that technical inspections require meticulous preparation before vehicles can board.

“We have to verify fuel levels, balance hazardous materials like vehicle batteries, and calculate exactly where each vehicle sits inside the cargo hold so the plane flies safely,” Bassett noted.

Bassett worked closely with Air Force air transportation specialists and flight loadmasters during joint inspections, using the live flights to mentor junior transportation management coordinators.

“What I’m most proud of is the real-world experience our junior transportation specialists gained,” Bassett said. “In our home brigade, we are surrounded by seasoned logisticians who can answer questions.”

Bassett added that young troops must be prepared to operate independently on future battlefields.

“As these young Soldiers advance, they may be sent to an isolated battalion where they are the only transportation expert on site,” Bassett noted. “Giving them these realistic repetitions now builds the confidence they need to advise commanders and solve complex shipping puzzles under pressure.”

While cargo planes departed Stewart Air National Guard Base, the brigade's road units executed one of the largest vehicle movements mounted by the New York National Guard in recent memory.

Capt. Marconi D’Auria-Gupta, commander of Charlie Company, 119th Division Sustainment Support Battalion, guided 40 tactical trucks organized into four separate travel groups along a 486-mile route traversing five states.

“Charlie Company’s road movement required months of mechanical preparation, borrowing supplemental fleet vehicles, and mapping detailed highway routes,” said Capt. Marconi D’Auria-Gupta. “We managed 40 heavy trucks in busy civilian traffic on Eastern Seaboard interstates, shared commercial truck stops for diesel refueling, and handled our own towing and mechanical repairs on the road.”

D’Auria-Gupta added that driver safety remained the overarching priority during the long transit.

“We safely and efficiently managed Soldier rest cycles while conducting a massive convoy along the eastern coast,” D’Auria-Gupta noted.

Coordinating hundreds of heavy military vehicles across crowded public highways required minute-by-minute tracking by the brigade's movement control cell.

“Movement control centers are where road plans meet real-world highway traffic,” said Maj. Yancey Reynoso, who directed the control cell. “Convoys encounter traffic delays, radio dead zones, and occasional mechanical breakdowns.”

Reynoso added that proactive tracking prevents small road problems from turning into operational failures.

“Our job is tracking vehicle locations, planning alternate detours, and coordinating breakdown support immediately so a stalled truck never stalls the overall mission,” Reynoso noted.

Upon arriving at Fort A.P. Hill, the brigade built a full division support area—a sprawling field logistical hub supplying fuel, water, ammunition, and field medical support to fighting units.

Soldiers worked through extreme summer heat, conducted night driving with night-vision goggles, tested long-range radio networks, and defended their perimeter against simulated ground attacks.

Col. Bryon L. Linnehan, commander of the 369th Division Sustainment Brigade, said the exercise proved the historic Harlem Hellfighters can rapidly mobilize, protect themselves, and sustain fighting units across great distances.

“Our consolidated annual training at Fort A.P. Hill gave Hellfighters the chance to prove our expeditionary capabilities in a tough, realistic setting,” Linnehan said.

“By moving troops by air and road with our Air National Guard partners, we sent a clear message that the 369th is ready to support the 42nd Infantry Division anywhere in the world,” he added.

Linnehan said that the training highlighted the importance of our various partnerships with allied nations, as some partners such as Sweden were invited to observe the complex large scale combat operations training.

items.title: Tanker fleet modernization will continue for decades, US Air Force officials say
items.author: Cristina Stassis
items.summary: “The last KC-135 pilot has not been born,” Air Mobility Command Deputy Commander Maj. Gen. Gerald Donohue said Tuesday.
items.body:
MilTech

Tanker fleet modernization will continue for decades, US Air Force officials say

A U.S. Air Force KC-135 Stratotanker refuels an F-35A Lightning II during Operation Epic Fury in the Central Command area of operations on April 5, 2026. (U.S. Air Force)

The U.S. Air Force will recapitalize aerial refueling tanker aircraft for decades longer and build new platforms for their sustainment in the meantime, service leaders and industry partners said Tuesday.

To support the tanker aircraft and the anticipated mission capability rates, the Air Force should continue prioritizing available spare parts and modernization efforts for the aircraft, officials and industry experts said during a panel at the Air & Space Forces Association’s 2026 Air, Space & Cyber Conference .

“The last KC-135 pilot has not been born,” Air Mobility Command Deputy Commander Maj. Gen. Gerald Donohue said during the panel, titled “Long-Range Airpower: Lessons from Midnight Hammer and Epic Fury.”

“That is just a statement of fact when you consider the time it takes to modernize, and so we will have to sustain our legacy platform as well as our newest platforms, and ensure that the joint force is supported by being able to execute the mission,” he continued.

The force primarily uses two tanker aircraft: the legacy KC-135 Stratotanker and the next-generation KC-46A Pegasus , which is in the first phase of recapitalization.

As the force continues to modernize its strategic bomber fleet, the service must increase optionality by modernizing the tanker fleet to better offer alternatives when needed.

Moving forward, recapitalization will be the command’s priority alongside modernization of existing aircraft, Donohue asserted, by emphasizing connectivity, survivability and technical viability.

“Epic Fury, Midnight Hammer underscore the importance that connectivity plays, not only to our own survivability, but more importantly, to the success of the joint force and the mission at hand, whether it’s passing information to the bomber force as they’re executing their refueling or to the combat air forces forward, we’ve got to have the connectivity to add that value,” Donohue said.

Donohue said that the service is currently going through recapitalization as it brings on the KC-46s and modernizes the KC-135s, highlighting that once the acquisition of the KC-46 is completed, the service will still have hundreds of KC-135s.

As future conflicts and operating areas get more and more contested, getting the bomber or fighter force to their last Air Refueling Control Time, or ARTC, puts the force at risk, he said, furthering the need for survival platforms with additional tanker systems that propel the viability of legacy and future aircraft.

“We can never walk away from the idea that our young airmen out there on the line today and for decades still will have to sustain 70-year-old-plus airframes,” Donohue said.

The panelists argued that partnership with industry matters most as the “biggest enabler” for getting capability into the hands of the warfighter faster and at a lower cost to the service, saying that more opportunities to rethink the work upfront boosts efficiency for the operator.

Jamie Burgess, Boeing’s vice president and general manager of Mobility, Surveillance and Bombers, said that the work the company did on the KC-46 aircraft, such as upgrades to the vision system for refueling, altered the way they think about the development work.

“Getting teams together — operators, subject matter experts, engineers — come to agreement on design up front so we can get after the detailed design work and get it built and tested and out to the operators,” he said in the panel.

Cristina Stassis is a reporter covering stories surrounding the defense industry, national security, military/veteran affairs and more. She previously worked as an editorial fellow for Defense News in 2024 where she assisted the newsroom in breaking news across Sightline Media Group.

items.title: Iran war has cost $38 billion, depleted two-thirds of US missile interceptors, CBO says
items.author: Natalie Oliverio
items.summary: The U.S. military has incurred about $38 billion in costs from combat operations against Iran, a new Congressional Budget Office analysis found.
items.body:
Global

Iran war has cost $38 billion, depleted two-thirds of US missile interceptors, CBO says

A U.S. Army air defense artilleryman conducts maintenance on an MIM-104 Patriot missile system in the Middle East. The Patriot is the Army’s primary terminal-phase anti-ballistic missile system. (U.S. Army)

The U.S. military has incurred about $38 billion in costs from combat operations against Iran through Aug. 1, while the conflict’s main opportunity cost has been the missile-defense interceptors the Pentagon has expended defending U.S. forces and allies, according to a new Congressional Budget Office analysis released today.

CBO estimates the conflict has consumed between one-half and two-thirds of the U.S. inventory of certain missile-defense interceptors since June 2025, leaving the military with fewer weapons available for a future conflict. Rebuilding those stocks could take at least five years, even if production rates increase, the agency found.

The estimate includes Patriot, Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD, Standard Missile-3 and Standard Missile-6 interceptors. CBO said the Pentagon does not disclose how many interceptors it has in its inventory. Instead, analysts compared reported expenditures with the total number of missiles DoD has purchased to estimate how much of the inventory has been used. The estimate applies to the combined inventory of those four interceptor systems.

Those interceptors accounted for $13.1 billion of the $21.7 billion CBO estimates the Pentagon would need to replace in munitions that were expended through Aug. 1. Land-attack cruise missiles accounted for another $7.3 billion, with $1.2 billion for other munitions.

A separate Defense Department inspector general report estimated the cost of the operation at $33.4 billion through June 29.

CBO said the campaign involved large expenditures of munitions during the first few weeks, particularly as U.S. forces defended against Iranian ballistic missile and drone attacks.

The interceptor depletion is particularly significant because the weapons are expensive and produced at relatively low rates. CBO estimates unit costs of roughly $4 million for a Patriot or SM-6, $12 million for a THAAD interceptor and $28 million for a sophisticated SM-3. The agency said the United States has already used significant quantities of these weapons defending Israel and then expended more during Operation Epic Fury.

That figure includes expended munitions, equipment losses, increased flying hours, other operations and higher fuel costs. It does not include costs borne by other federal agencies or military operating costs already included in the federal budget.

The highest costs beyond munitions were $10.4 billion for increased flying hours, $2.7 billion for fuel and $1.9 billion to replace equipment lost in battle. The equipment losses included a THAAD radar destroyed by Iran.

The initial phase of Operation Epic Fury involved about 250 tactical aircraft, including roughly 90 from two carrier strike groups, as well as an amphibious ready group. Those forces were supported by bombers, airlifters, refueling tankers, other Navy vessels and Army air-defense, aviation and artillery units.

CBO said the Pentagon did not respond to its requests for information, so analysts relied on government databases and public reports. The agency cautioned that its estimate is therefore subject to considerable uncertainty.

The administration had requested $87.6 billion in supplemental funding in June, including $67.1 billion for the DoD, with $42.3 billion identified as directly related to the conflict. That portion was about 10% higher than CBO’s estimate.

The cost of the conflict also continues to grow. CBO estimates each additional month of fighting would cost roughly $2 billion to $3 billion if the intensity remains relatively low, with costs potentially higher if operations intensify.

The depleted interceptor stocks could pose a particular problem in a conflict with China, CBO said, because Beijing maintains large numbers of ballistic and cruise missiles.

Natalie Oliverio is an independent journalist and Navy veteran who covers military and veterans’ issues. Drawing on her experience as a talent executive and mentor, she writes about the policies, people and programs shaping the military community.

items.title: Space Force Accepting Applications for Interservice Transfers Until Oct. 2
items.author: Greg Hadley
items.summary: For the next few weeks, the Space Force is accepting applications from Airmen, Soldiers, Sailors, and Marines who want to become Guardians. The post Space Force Accepting Applications for Interservice Transfers Until Oct. 2 appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

For the next 17 days, the Space Force is accepting applications from Airmen, Soldiers, Sailors, and Marines to transfer into the Space Force and become Guardians.

The first interservice transfer window in three years opened Sept. 15 and closes Oct. 2. The Space Force is looking for “several hundred” new mid-grade officers and enlisted members during this period, a Department of the Air Force spokesperson said. Only Active-Duty members are eligible; members of the various Reserve and National Guard components, as well as the Coast Guard and Merchant Marine are not.

Any service member can apply, even those with no experience in space operations. But priority will be given to those not requiring retraining into one of the Space Force’s three main operator career fields—space, cyber, and intelligence. Also of interest: acquisition and engineering officers.

The Space Force provided a cross-service map detailing how Army, Navy, Air Force, and Marine Corps specialties align with Space Force job codes.

Individuals with “derogatory information” in their file or are on any sort of administrative or medical hold will also be disqualified.

To transfer, service members must submit a service career brief, their last five performance reports, their most recent physical fitness and body composition assessment, and an endorsement for transfer from their unit commander. Interested members must also submit documentation of any approved religious or medical accommodations they have received, and whether they have been selected for promotion.

The price of a transfer: a four-year service commitment upon joining the Space Force.

The Space Force was formed by transferring members, with most transferring from the Air Force. Then it held interservice transfer windows in each of three fiscal years, 2022, 2023, and 2024. USSF accepted 720 transfers in 2022 , 511 in 2023, and 148 in 2024.

In 2025, the Space Force took in transfers from the Air National Guard and Air Force Reserve, and at the same time created a new hybrid full-time/part-time system under the Space Force Personnel Management Act. Around 300 Guardsmen and Reservists transferred to the Space Force on a full-time basis, and nearly 250 joined as part-timers.

Now, as the Space Force embarks on doubling the force from about 10,000 to 20,000 uniformed Guardians in the next five years, interservice transfers are back on the table.

USSF continues to benefit from extremely high interest from the public and has consistently met or exceeded its recruiting goals every year since its start in 2019. Interservice transfers of mid-grade enlisted and officer personnel are essential, however, to ensuring the Space Force maintains an appropriate mix of junior, mid-grade, and senior personnel.

The department spokesperson said the focus on mid-grade transfers is necessary “to meet our … requirements and account for the service’s steep growth as projected.”

items.title: Iranian strikes damaged hundreds of US military buildings, dozens of aircraft
items.author: Michael Peck
items.summary: Iranian strikes have damaged hundreds of U.S. military and diplomatic buildings, as well as dozens of aircraft, a Pentagon watchdog said.
items.body:
Pentagon

Iranian strikes damaged hundreds of US military buildings, dozens of aircraft

Smoke rises after Iran carried out a missile strike on the main headquarters of the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet in Manama, Bahrain, in retaliation against U.S.-Israeli attacks on Feb. 28, 2026. (Anadolu via Getty Images)

Iranian strikes have damaged hundreds of U.S. military and diplomatic buildings, according to a new report by the Department of Defense Office of the Inspector General.

U.S. Central Command told IG investigators that “Iranian strikes damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan during the conflict.”

While the report provided no details on damaged military facilities, it did include specifics on damage to U.S. diplomatic facilities.

The State Department told investigators that “U.S. diplomatic facilities in four countries suffered physical damage from Iranian strikes, with an estimated total cost of about $184 million.”

U.S. diplomatic sites in Iraq suffered more than 600 attacks, while the embassies in Kuwait City and Riyadh were also hit.

Operation Epic Fury had cost the United States $33.4 billion as of June 29, based on Pentagon estimates. The amount includes $22.3 billion in expended munitions, $3.7 billion in equipment losses and $7.4 billion in costs beyond CENTCOM’s normal operating expenses.

However, these estimates do not count the costs of repairing infrastructure.

The Department of Defense “did not include the cost of military construction for damaged infrastructure in its estimate because the DoD has not determined what its future posture will be in the region, how it will construct its bases, and what percentage of the construction costs allies and partners will contribute,” the report states.

Because Congress did not appropriate funds for the war in Iran, the money is being funneled from normal operating budgets, such as amounts set aside for training and maintenance.

“The absence of a dedicated appropriation for OEF means that it can be difficult to calculate the total ‘cost’ of OEF,” noted the report, which is among the first official assessments of Operation Epic Fury since it began on Feb. 28.

Funding is also becoming an issue for U.S. Transportation Command, which flew more than 1,500 missions to support the mission.

“During peak OEF times, airlift surged to 30 to 40 daily missions directly into the CENTCOM [area of responsibility], with an additional 20 to 30 daily aircraft pushing into the USEUCOM AOR for transload operations,” the report said.

This cost nearly $2.4 billion as of June 30.

“While these obligations have been largely reimbursed by the military services to date, USTRANSCOM reported that it anticipates delayed payments moving forward as service funding is depleted without a supplemental appropriation,” the IG said.

The report confirmed that dozens of U.S. manned and unmanned aircraft have been destroyed or damaged, based on data from a Congressional Research Service report released in May and “vetted” by CENTCOM as of Aug. 24.

The tally of destroyed aircraft includes four F-15Es, one A-10, four AH-6 helicopters, one AH-64 and one MH-60, as well as an MQ-4C drone and as many as 30 MQ-9 Reapers.

The report listed 18 dead U.S. military personnel as of Aug. 27. The Pentagon claimed 417 wounded as of June 30, though casualty figures released in late August soared to 774.

Michael Peck is a correspondent for Defense News and a columnist for the Center for European Policy Analysis. He holds an M.A. in political science from Rutgers University. Find him at theuncommondefense.com. His email is mikedefense1@gmail.com.
