items.title: AFRL demonstrates modular multimode propulsion system for sustained space maneuver
items.author: Patrick Londergan
items.summary: EDWARDS AIR FORCE BASE, Calif. -- The Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) recently demonstrated an innovative spacecraft propulsion system under realistic conditions in a specialized test facility at Edwards Air Force Base, California. “This work helps advance propulsion technologies that will give future space operators more flexible options for maneuver to adapt and sustain operations in demanding environments, as is required by U.S. Space Command,” said Dr. Andrew Williams , director of the
items.body:
EDWARDS AIR FORCE BASE, Calif. -- The Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) recently demonstrated an innovative spacecraft propulsion system under realistic conditions in a specialized test facility at Edwards Air Force Base, California.

“This work helps advance propulsion technologies that will give future space operators more flexible options for maneuver to adapt and sustain operations in demanding environments, as is required by U.S. Space Command,” said Dr. Andrew Williams , director of the AFRL Space Warfare Directorate .

Termed Propulsion Optimization UNifying Chemical and Electric (POUNCE), the demonstration proved the capability of an innovative propulsion technology called Modular Multimode Propulsion (MMP). MMP features both electric and chemical propulsion using the same propellant along with a single tank and feed system. Electric propulsion enables high-efficiency, low-thrust, long-duration and slow maneuvers; chemical propulsion enables shorter-duration, higher-thrust and faster maneuvers.

For the team behind POUNCE, the effort is not just about proving a concept—it is about giving future operators more flexible tools to meet mission demands in space.

“This demonstration is a pioneering leap in the advancement of flexible, modular and high-performance space propulsion technology to enable dynamic space operations,” said Dr. Javier Urzay, AFRL Rocket and Space Propulsion Division chief. “Our goal is to bring the future faster and deliver integrated capabilities for space warfare.”

The MMP architecture reduces system mass and volume, while increasing operational flexibility and resilience. It provides operators with discretion to allocate the same propellant to high-tempo maneuvers or more efficient repositioning of orbital assets.

The propellant used for the MMP system in this demonstration was the AFRL-developed Advanced Spacecraft Energetic Non-Toxic (ASCENT) fuel. AFRL has pursued several technology maturation activities jointly with industry to exploit the higher-density specific impulse and safer handling of ASCENT for spacecraft propulsion.

POUNCE’s MMP system also incorporated hardware from industry partners, including a composite conformal tank and propellant feed system from Flight Works, chemical thrusters from Igneon Aerospace, and a PALOMINO ion array electrospray thruster from Revolution Space.

“Alongside the relationships with our commercial partners, another equally important ingredient for this demonstration is the unique capabilities offered by the Space Propulsion Environment Facility (SPEF) at the AFRL Rocket Lab at Edwards AFB,” said Dr. Gregory Yandek, AFRL In-Space Propulsion Branch chief.

Inside SPEF, researchers were able to expose the experimental MMP system to the high-vacuum characteristics of orbital environments. Theorists first conceptualized the dual-mode combination of low-thrust and high-thrust propulsion capabilities for space missions in the 1960s, but experimentation with hardware has been limited to single-mode or primitive components until now.

Finally, the POUNCE MMP demonstration highlights how leveraging public-private partnerships can accelerate the transition of technology concepts toward operationally relevant capabilities. The demonstration hardware featured a highly modular design to quickly and easily swap different propulsion subsystems without having to change the parent system. This extra layer of flexibility will greatly increase system life replenishment and space maneuver capabilities in future operating environments.

About AFRL

The Air Force Research Laboratory is the Department of the Air Force’s primary scientific research and development center and one of six centers within Air Force Materiel Command. AFRL leads the discovery, development and delivery of technologies for air, space and multidomain. With a workforce spanning seven mission areas at more than 40 locations worldwide, AFRL conducts research ranging from basic science to advanced technology development. For more information, visit afresearchlab.com .

items.title: The Recent Rise of Women Gun Owners
items.summary: In recent years, women made up almost half of all new gun owners, a striking shift from the historical norm, when women accounted for about a quarter of them. And the uptick is widespread across geographic and demographic subgroups.
items.body:
Commentary

Sep 11, 2026

By Rosanna Smart and Andrew R. Morral

This commentary was originally published by Vital City on September 9, 2026.

For generations, gun ownership in America has been a man's world. But that's changing, and fast. Between 2020 and 2022, more than 7.5 million people bought their first gun, and an estimated 60 million new firearms entered the U.S. civilian market. An unprecedented number of these purchasers were women. In recent years, women made up almost half of all new gun owners , a striking shift from the historical norm, when women accounted for about 24% of gun owners. While previous reports on increased gun ownership among women have been overstated , our analysis confirms a notable uptick in female gun ownership that was widespread across geographic and demographic subgroups. What remains unknown are the implications of this trend for public health and safety.

The General Social Survey (GSS) is a large, nationally representative survey of adults in the United States, conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago; it has asked about household and personal gun ownership roughly every two years for the past five decades. The GSS also asks about a wide range of social, economic and political measures, supporting descriptions of how ownership trends have varied across subgroups and how the landscape of gun ownership may or may not be changing. (An important note: These are survey data and thus subject to error if people do not know or are unwilling to disclose whether they own guns. But because there are no administrative datasets that capture gun ownership or sales, survey data are the best we have to work with.)

Based on the GSS, women's personal ownership of firearms increased substantially in recent years. After more than a decade of stable gun ownership, women's ownership rose starkly between 2018 and 2021, going from 10% of adult women owning guns in 2018 to 15% in 2021, then up again slightly to 16% by 2024. Other national surveys, such as Pew's American Trends Panel, report similar trends in women's gun ownership over this period (although prevalence estimates differ from GSS, likely due to differences in question wording and sampling). Over the same period, men's gun ownership remained relatively flat; the percentage of men who own guns as of 2024 (36%) is now quite a bit lower than the ownership rate from two decades prior (40%). The result is a continued narrowing of the gender gap in gun ownership, which has fallen from 29 percentage points in 2004 to 19 percentage points in 2024.…

The remainder of this commentary is available at vitalcitynyc.org .

Rosanna Smart is a senior economist at RAND and codirector of the RAND Drug Policy Research Center and RAND Gun Policy in America initiative. She was selected as the 2025 Mark Kleiman Memorial Lecturer. Andrew R. Morral is RAND's Greenwald Family Chair in Gun Policy Research, director of the National Collaborative on Gun Violence Research, and codirector of RAND's Gun Policy in America initiative.

items.title: Who Benefits from Education Savings Accounts? Q&A with Susha Roy
items.summary: Tens of thousands of American families use state-funded education savings accounts for their children's education. How exactly do these accounts work? Who benefits from them? And how do they affect education funding more broadly?
items.body:
Who Benefits from Education Savings Accounts? Q&A with Susha Roy

Commentary

Sep 11, 2026

Tens of thousands of American families have some decisions to make as a new school year begins. They hold state-funded education savings accounts, which give them wide latitude to choose how to educate their children.

Such accounts have been around for years, mostly as a way to help students with disabilities get the specialized services they need. But a growing number of states have made them available to all families. Federal tax credits kicking in this year will also allow families to write off up to $1,700 to scholarship-granting organizations for similar education services and expenses.

What all this will mean for students, their academic achievement, and the future of public schools is still far from clear.

Susha Roy has been looking for answers in one of the states that pioneered education savings accounts, Arizona. She’s a policy researcher at RAND and a specialist in school choice policies. Her findings could help other states ensure their programs are helping the students they want to help, without leaving some behind.

Let’s start with the basics. What are education savings accounts, and how do they work?

They essentially take the money that would have been allocated for a student in public school and make it available directly to the family. The family can then use it on any sort of educational expense. That could be private school tuition, tutoring services, homeschooling expenses, textbooks—you name it.

Your research has shown that these accounts can be game changers for some students. Who benefits from them?

There are two main categories of students who have typically benefited from these. The first is students in underperforming neighborhood schools. These accounts give them the flexibility to pursue something outside of their local public school, and that can be really important for them.

The other category is students with disabilities. There are all kinds of special needs that public schools are very well equipped to support. But there are also disabilities that require very individualized and specialized support. Our research in Arizona found that a large number of students with autism use these accounts, for example. The support they need can be so varied that public schools might not be able to meet their needs. These accounts may be really helpful for them.

There have also been concerns about “cream skimming” as states make these accounts available to everyone. What is that, and how might these accounts encourage it?

Cream skimming is when private schools and other schools of choice enroll students who are higher achieving or more affluent or just easier to educate than the general student population. We found a pretty clear pattern of this in Arizona: Students using these accounts tended to live in wealthier neighborhoods and came from higher-achieving public school districts. They weren’t necessarily reflective of the population of students who you might think could benefit the most from these education savings accounts.

Now, early adopters of any education program are often different from the general population. But what this does suggest to me is that policy design is really important here. We shouldn’t expect that all kids and families will know how to take advantage of these new accounts. If states want to expand access to educational opportunities for all students, they could consider prioritizing outreach to families who could benefit the most.

If states want to expand access to educational opportunities for all students, they could consider prioritizing outreach to families who could benefit the most.

How do these accounts affect funding for public schools and the broader education system?

Most states tie state funding for public schools to student enrollment. So if students opt out of going to their public school, that is going to decrease the state funds the school will receive. Maybe the school can save money by not hiring as many teachers, since it won’t have as many students. But it still has fixed costs, like building maintenance, and that can become a real challenge.

What we saw in Arizona, though, was that a lot of the students who received these accounts were already in private school. And we found evidence that private school tuition went up when these accounts became available. We need more research here, but it could be that schools raised their tuition to try to capture the additional state funding that families had coming in.

It goes back to how you design these programs. If there are no accountability mechanisms, you might just inflate the cost of private school and subsidize families whose kids were already going to private school anyway without making sure the quality of those schools also improves.

If you were advising state leaders who were considering accounts like these, what would you tell them?

Collect data on how students with these accounts perform in their receiving schools. Without that, we just won’t know for sure whether the money states spend on education savings accounts benefits children.

I’ve had some encouraging conversations with some states that are trying to be really thoughtful about this. A few have talked about having a student ID that stays with students as they move between sectors. That would allow you to track student outcomes in a way that we really can’t right now.

It’s critically important that states’ highly consequential policy decisions are informed by good evidence. That’s why we do this work at RAND. There’s such a huge opportunity to help states shape these important policy decisions so they benefit their constituents.

items.title: Public procurement and AI governance
items.author: Afek Shamir
items.summary: This report examines how AI middle powers can use public procurement to govern frontier AI. It develops a set of procurement guarantees, and assesses whether coordinated purchasing standards could strengthen state bargaining power.
items.body:
This report assesses public procurement as an AI governance tool, develops contractual guarantees for state buyers, and examines whether coordination among AI middle powers could strengthen bargaining leverage, evaluation capacity and resilience to AI crises.

Public procurement and AI governance

Developing a strategic framework for middle powers

Afek Shamir

Research Published Sep 11, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Frontier AI capabilities are concentrated among a small number of private firms headquartered in the United States and China. For states which neither develop nor host leading models, this concentration creates a dependence on foreign AI providers whose capabilities they often cannot independently evaluate and whose technology may be constrained by the laws of the provider’s home jurisdiction.

Public procurement offers ‘AI middle powers’ one mechanism for governing these dependencies. These are states with significant economic, diplomatic, security or regulatory capabilities that nevertheless depend technologically on foreign frontier AI firms. The report finds that three categories of risk fall disproportionately on state buyers in AI middle powers : vendor lock-in and the threat of service withdrawal, limited visibility into frontier AI development, and data sovereignty and information-security risks.

To mitigate these risks, the report develops a framework of procurement obligations that governments could seek to negotiate with AI providers. These include model access for evaluation, information sharing, funding for reliability research, state-of-the-art risk management requirements, termination and exit provisions, and measures to support domestic and allied capability.

The analysis finds that public procurement is a useful but bounded mechanism for governing frontier AI. Governments are not yet major customers of frontier AI firms, and leading developers may be able to forego government contracts rather than accept costly requirements. Procurement contracts with foreign providers may also remain subordinate to the national-security laws of a vendor’s home state, and state buyers can face persistent information asymmetries when negotiating with leading technology companies. At the same time, government demand for frontier AI is growing, and public-sector contracts offer firms more than revenue alone. They provide financial predictability and a degree of prestige and regulatory validation, making governments strategically important customers even if they are not yet indispensable to firms’ business models.

The central recommendation is that AI middle powers should assess whether collective coordination on procurement requirements can strengthen their bargaining position and state capacity.

Key Takeaways

Short-term actions (actions that could be initiated within 12 months):

Firstly, governments should begin with a shared assessment of the risks that procurement requirements are intended to address. Participating states should compare the risks they associate with different government uses of frontier AI, including but not limited to dependence on individual foreign providers, loss of access, insufficient visibility into model behaviour, and requirements for data control. Common procurement provisions should follow predominantly where separate governments assess risks similarly.

Secondly, governments should assess the most suitable institutional arrangement for procurement coordination. The G7, the EU, NATO, and International Network of AI Safety Institutes already provide mechanisms for cooperation on AI policy, standards and technical evaluation. A dedicated arrangement may be justified where no current institution combines sufficient purchasing relevance and technical capacity.

Thirdly, smaller middle powers which lack state access to frontier AI should explore opportunities to pool demand with partners and strengthen their negotiating position. Where an individual government is unlikely to represent sufficient demand to influence a frontier AI provider, cooperation with other buyers could increase the commercial significance of their purchasing preferences and requirements.

Medium- to long-term actions (actions likely to require approximately 1–5 years or longer):

Firstly, governments should identify which AI capabilities need to remain available independently of any single foreign provider and invest selectively in the infrastructure required to preserve them. For most middle powers, this is unlikely to mean reproducing the full frontier AI stack nationally. A more realistic strategy could include building a meaningful share of domestic or allied compute, creating secure hosting facilities, securing access to multiple model families for optionality reasons, and bringing in technical talent to government with expertise in fine-tuning and the know-how to migrate critical workloads. These assets would also strengthen bargaining power by making the future option of switching providers more credible.

Secondly, governments should strengthen their capacity to evaluate and assure frontier AI systems. This includes developing assurance and technical AI expertise within defence agencies and supporting the creation of a mature third-party evaluation and assurance sector. These capabilities are necessary to make procurement guarantees practically enforceable.

Thirdly, procurement coordination could provide a basis for wider cooperation on AI incidents and resilience to AI-related failures. Governments that establish common procurement requirements would have an existing mechanism for sharing information with one another and with providers. Over time, this could support common approaches to incident reporting and exercises for responding to significant AI-related incidents.

Geopolitical Strategic Competition

Military Acquisition and Procurement

items.title: JBER NCO plays for winning team in Armed Forces softball championship
items.author: A1C Thomas Polk
items.summary: It’s a hot Oklahoma day, and it’s the final game in the 2026 Armed Forces Softball Championship. The men’s Air Force team is up against the Army. It has been a challenging few days leading up to this point–but U.S. Air Force Staff Sgt. Jacob McDonald, representing not only the Air Force as a whole but also his home base of JBER, is sure his team has what it takes to bring home the gold.
items.body:
JOINT BASE ELMENDORF-RICHARDSON, Alaska – It’s a hot Oklahoma day, and it’s the final game in the 2026 Armed Forces Softball Championship. The men’s Air Force team is up against the Army. It has been a challenging few days leading up to this point–but U.S. Air Force Staff Sgt. Jacob McDonald, representing not only the Air Force as a whole but also his home base of JBER, is sure his team has what it takes to bring home the gold.

McDonald is right. Despite fierce competition, as the sun beats down overhead and players bake in the 100-degree heat, and McDonald’s friends and family cheer him on thousands of miles away, the Air Force team secures the win as the 2026 champions.

The Armed Forces Softball Championship is an annual tournament separated into men's and women's brackets, and the 2026 event featured Army, Navy and Air Force teams. This year it was held at Devon Park in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, from Aug. 26 through Aug. 29. The Air Force men’s team had 15 players, selected due to their sports experience, participation in military games and personal references.

For McDonald, his softball career began well before the championship. The noncommissioned officer in charge of the 673d Logistics Readiness Squadron commander support staff at JBER, he used his history in competitive softball, service experience and the support from his friends and family to perform and earn his spot on this year’s team.

He said competing alongside the other branches of the Department of War provided him the opportunity to rise to the challenge and build camaraderie at the same time.

“I started playing competitive softball at my first duty station, Kadena Air Base in Okinawa, Japan, eight years ago,” said McDonald. “Getting the opportunity to represent the Air Force in the Armed Forces Softball Championship has been a goal I’ve set for myself since joining the military.”

While stationed at JBER, McDonald traveled to the Lower 48 often to participate in civilian and military tournaments. In doing so, he gained valuable training, experience, and recognition from other players and coaches.

“This was the first year I got the opportunity to put in an application package, and it was everything I imagined it would be,” he said.

McDonald’s softball and operational experience allowed him to quickly adapt to his new team and work together towards a common goal. Throughout his time at the tournament, he built camaraderie not only with his teammates but also with his competition. “It goes from not knowing each other to ending up being brothers and feeling like family,” said McDonald.

The men’s Air Force team went into the final championship games with a record of five wins and one loss. In the finals, the Air Force faced the Army and came out victorious with a score of 33-18.

While McDonald had his team to rely on at the championship, he also had those back home to cheer him on.

“They're very supportive and responsive, from my leadership all the way to my friends, and especially my wife,” he said. “She was the one who pushed me to do it, and that definitely helped, going out there and knowing that I have as much support as I did.”

Those who know McDonald have spoken to the quality of his character. His supervisor, Master Sgt. Daviea Cowans, quality assurance superintendent of the 673d Logistics Readiness Squadron, said that he is respectful and professional. Even during the live stream of the games, Cowans watched as McDonald “made sure his teammates were looked after,” continuing to display his dedication to his team.

“He is personable, charismatic and cares about the Airmen he supports,” said Cowans. “He always takes on any task and works to the best of his ability.”

McDonald said he took everything that he had learned over the years as an Airman and competitive softball player and highlighted what the Air Force represents: integrity, service and excellence.

“It’s an honor to be able to wear the ‘Air Force’ across my chest and be one of the few selected to go out there and represent not only JBER and my squadron, but the Air Force as a whole,” said McDonald. “It’s a great experience, and there's definitely a lot of pride that goes into that.”

items.title: Framework for the Opioid Use Disorder Cascade of Care
items.author: Katherine E. Watkins
items.summary: We sought to adapt the framework under the constraints of electronic health record data and identify patient populations at risk for opioid use disorder treatment discontinuity.
items.body:
Adaptation and Application for a Large Municipal Health System

Mariah Kalmin , Christina Crowley , Lia Pak , Colleen M. McCullough , Beth Ann Griffin , Kyle Ragins , Hrishikesh Belani , Katherine E. Watkins

Research Posted on rand.org Sep 10, 2026 Published in: Public Health Reports® (2026). DOI: 10.1177/00333549261467293

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Objectives

Most people with opioid use disorder (OUD) do not receive effective treatments despite their existence. The OUD cascade of care framework can be used to inform quality improvement efforts to address this gap, but data access and linkage requirements may limit its use. We sought to adapt the framework under the constraints of electronic health record data and identify patient populations at risk for OUD treatment discontinuity.

Materials and Methods

We extracted data on patients with OUD from the Los Angeles County Department of Health Services from July 2022 through June 2023. We adapted the cascade of care to include probable OUD diagnosis, receipt of naloxone prescription, and receipt of ≥1 and ≥2 buprenorphine prescriptions. We then stratified and conducted statistical analyses for associations by sex, race and ethnicity, and facility type (inpatient, primary care, emergency, or urgent care).

Results

Of 3881 patients identified with probable OUD, 49% received a naloxone prescription and 30% and 17% had ≥1 and ≥2 buprenorphine prescriptions, respectively, in 1 year. Non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic patients were less likely to receive buprenorphine prescriptions than were non-Hispanic White patients and patients of other or unknown race and ethnicity. We observed larger gaps in care between receipt of ≥1 and ≥2 buprenorphine prescriptions for patients using urgent care and emergency departments compared with patients in other settings.

Practice Implications

This study illustrates substantial gaps between OUD diagnosis and treatment. This adapted framework for the OUD cascade of care can serve as a quality-monitoring tool to aid clinicians and health care administrators in narrowing the treatment gap for people with OUD.

items.title: Mediators of the Effects of an HIV Prevention Advocacy Training Intervention on Prevention Advocacy Among Persons Living with HIV in Uganda
items.author: Stephen Okoboi
items.summary: In a secondary analysis from a randomized controlled trial of a peer advocacy training intervention for PLWH, we examined mediators of intervention effects on HIV prevention advocacy across members of their social network.
items.body:
Glenn Wagner , Laura M. Bogart , Joseph K. Matovu , Violet Gwokyalya , Harold D. Green , Susan Ninsiima , David J. Klein , Stephen Okoboi

Research Posted on rand.org Sep 10, 2026 Published in: Journal of Behavioral Medicine (2026). DOI: 10.1007/s10865-026-00704-z

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Pathways through which advocacy training enhances engagement in advocacy among persons living with HIV (PLWH) are not well understood. In a secondary analysis from a randomized controlled trial of a peer advocacy training intervention for PLWH, we examined mediators of intervention effects on HIV prevention advocacy (i.e., encouraging others to engage in HIV protective behaviors) across members of their social network. A sample of 210 PLWH (105 in each of the intervention and control arms) provided information about their advocacy to their social network members at baseline, and 6-, 12-, and 18-month follow-up. Repeated measures linear regressions showed that PLWH in the intervention group targeted more social network members with advocacy for HIV testing, condom use, pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) use, HIV care, and ART use over the follow-up period compared to those in the control group. In path analysis that examined each mediator in a separate model, reduced internalized HIV stigma and increased HIV knowledge as measured at month 6, each fully mediated the intervention effect on HIV care advocacy; reduced stigma partially mediated the effects on advocacy targeting each of the other four HIV protective behaviors, while increased knowledge partially mediated effects on HIV testing, condom and PrEP use advocacy. Results were unchanged when examining the joint mediation of stigma and knowledge. HIV disclosure and advocacy self-efficacy had no mediating effect. These findings highlight the importance of helping PLWH to cope with HIV stigma and gain knowledge about basic facts and common misconceptions related to HIV, to propel their engagement in advocacy for multiple HIV protective behaviors within their social networks.

items.title: UK Armed Forces pay tribute to late King of Norway at his funeral in Oslo
items.summary: Royal Marines and British Army personnel attended the funeral of King Harald V of Norway on Wednesday.
items.body:
Royal Marines and British Army personnel attended the funeral of King Harald V of Norway on Wednesday.

20 Royal Marines provided a marching detachment lining the route of the funeral procession in Oslo. Personnel from 1st Battalion, The Yorkshire Regiment, also attended as part of the UK’s tribute.

The late King, who died on 28 August, maintained a dedicated 45-year relationship with the British Armed Forces as an Honorary Colonel in the UK Royal Marines and an Honorary General in the British Army. He met with UK Commando Forces leadership every year and maintained a sharp, active interest in the Corps.

King Harald V’s father, King Olav V, was appointed an Honorary Admiral in the Royal Navy in 1958. In 1961, he and his son, the then Crown Prince Harald, were hosted onboard the Royal Navy aircraft carrier HMS Hermes during her regional engagement visit to Oslo.

The then Crown Prince Harald was appointed Honorary Colonel of the Royal Marines in March 1981 by Her Late Majesty Queen Elizabeth II, the first such appointment involving a member of a foreign Royal household in the Corps’ history. He paid his first visit to the Royal Marines that October, touring CTCRM Lympstone and RM Bickleigh, where he watched a cliff assault by 40 Commando and a demonstration of jungle warfare training by 42 Commando.

His connection with the Royal Marines continued throughout his reign. In 2018, he visited Royal Marines from X Company, 45 Commando, at Vaernes Camp in Norway during Exercise Trident Juncture, NATO’s largest collective defence exercise in a decade, where he was briefed on the Corps’ role in the exercise and joined celebrations marking the Royal Marines’ 354th birthday.

items.title: Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard MP's speech at Mansion House Defence and Security event
items.summary: Minister Pollard highlighting the importance of collaboration between government, industry and private finance, to strengthen UK deterrence and drive economic growth.
items.body:
Lady Mayor, thank you very much for hosting this event today and good afternoon, everyone. It’s a real pleasure to be with you today.

Under this one roof we have many leaders and decision makers needed to spark that next generation of defence innovation that we need to keep our country safe and support our allies. So, thank you for giving up your valuable time to be here.

I’m honoured that I get to speak as warm up act to my friend, the Ukrainian Ambassador. I’ve spent a lot of time in Kyiv over the past two years in particular, and the courage of the Ukrainian people is something that we must honour not just in words but in the actual support that we provide for their frontline, for their nation, for the innovators and we do that by not just sending equipment to Ukraine but by partnering, innovating and developing new technologies together.

I know that there are people in this room whose work is not theoretical in that regard and you are making a big difference to our friends in Ukraine so thank you for what you do.

Now, we meet at a point where global geopolitics is more fragile, more disruptive and more changeable. And that means we need an entirely new system of warfighting and deterrence, which means more innovation and new approaches with new weapon systems that revolutionised the battlefield.

Certainly, the way that the United Kingdom would now fight is fundamentally different today than it was at the point when Putin launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine only those four and a half years ago. We’re learning the lessons from Ukraine by supporting them, but that means changing the way that the United Kingdom operates.

Now, our most urgent mission right now is to transform Britain’s defence posture and turbocharge innovation. Many of the most critical advances in defence right now are coming from tech startups and tech scale-ups. Agile businesses which are seizing the opportunities on offer and driving change at speed. And so today our challenge is this: how can we get better at finding, funding and firing up the most creative minds and enterprise to get the best technology into the hands of our armed forces and those of our allies as fast as possible.

Now it was just over two years ago that this government took office and we inherited a defence programme which to be honest and to be frank was unfit to counter the dangers that we now face. We are moving towards warfighting readiness and in doing so we must discard the warm comfort blanket that we are used to in Britain, of polishing old things and pretending that that will protect us. If our technology and kit will not work in Ukraine, I do not want it in our armed forces. That is an opportunity for new technology, new thinking, new weapons to be brought to the fore. And in designing new technology, we need to design for the conflicts of today and the battles of tomorrow.

Now, our supply chains are critical to that. An industry that works in our supply chains know how painfully slow, wasteful and costly the procurement the MOD previously undertook was. We are changing that. I think it was especially true for those small businesses and scale-ups with amazing products who struggled sometimes to find the right buyer within the MOD.

Now since that time, we’ve produced a new blueprint for a completely different type of military and a different type of procurement. We published our Strategic Defence Review, Defence Industrial Strategy and Defence Investment Plan to build a more resilient and warfighting-ready military, backed by a world-class supply chain and we’re bringing industry into the heart of defence the fundamental enabler of everything that we are trying to achieve. To not only make our country more secure, but also more successful and prosperous, by creating high-quality defence jobs, skills and opportunities in every postcode.

I used to be incentivised by the MOD press office to say defence is an engine for growth in all my interviews, they used to be encouraging me to do it. With Andy Burnham in Downing Street I now say re-industrialisation, but the fundamental truth is there. Investment in defence creates good jobs. It provides opportunities in particular for our young people and we should be unafraid and unapologetic of saying that truth loudly. Defence spending is an engine for growth. It is a way of re-industrialising. It is a way of creating opportunity. It also keeps us safe.

Now to make our country more secure and more successful we need to create more high quality defence jobs, skills and opportunities. Now if we are to do that SMEs in particular, scale-ups, are really important. Within the MOD, we’ve reformed our system with a new National Armaments Director, Rupert Pearce, coming from a FTSE 100 company, bringing a new corporate approach and energy to the way that we procure.

We’ve established the Defence Office of Small Business growth to help remove those obstacles to entry, cut red tape, and roll out a 50% increase in spend from the MOD with medium and small-sized firms by Summer 2028. That’s moving an extra two and a half billion pounds into the pockets of SMEs by changing the way we procure, making it easier for small businesses to enter our supply chain.

We’ve published our SME Action Plan to set out what we will do so we can be held accountable for that change, and that supports start-ups, scale-ups, and other companies to be able to grow. And helping small firms navigate the routes to funding is something crucial if you want to get the best out of them. At a national level our Defence Office for Small Business Growth provides the guidance for those routes, removes duplication when we find it and clarifies the entry points where necessary.

At local levels I’m really pleased that the rollout of regional defence and security clusters have been so successful with more regions developing them, creating new regional routes to tailor support for businesses and bring together localised networks of major suppliers, devolved and local governments and importantly provide a forum for investors to meet them and support them as well.

Now, Ukraine has shown us the way to innovate at lightning speed because of the necessity of the war that they are fighting. And as we learn from Ukraine’s lead, defence must harness the resources that Britain possesses not just across tech and engineering sectors, but across finance, consulting and academia as well - to help create, inspire and deliver the change that we need. And finance is obviously key to our topic today.

Now, the government is already increasing defence spending. As a defence minister, of course, I would like more defence spending. But it’s not just from the taxpayer that there’s opportunities for investing in defence. It’s how you crowd in private capital, how you use the institutions, the networks, the structures of the City of London and the UK’s place at the heart of global financial trade, to bring more private capital into defence, creating more good jobs and more deterrence. Now, public investment will remain central to that mission as we increase our defence capabilities. But in a more dangerous world, we need to build more capacity now, rather than just wait for the increase in defence money that we know is coming over the next 10 years.

So that’s why the Defence Investment Plan sets out the priority areas that we will invest in both now, and later to provide the certainty for investors to understand what type of technologies, what areas of defence will the government invest in, where we also seek investment from the private sector.

And we need to work hard to make sure that Defence and our colleagues in the investment community speak the same language. Because I think, at the moment, there’s a risk that we sometimes speak past each other. And speaking the same language with the same necessary data will increase our ability to deliver.

Now, Britain has long prospered when government, industry and finance have worked together and our task today is not to reinvent the finance sectors, but a way of bringing us together to create that new partnership for today’s era.

Now, the prize is significant, not just stronger national defence and security, but a more innovative defence sector and a growing market that helps re-industrialise, but also an opportunity to export to our friends as well. Because it’s not just the United Kingdom that’s investing in defence. Our allies in NATO and further afield are doing the same.

Now, in the Defence Investment Plan, we announced a Defence Investment Unit because investors need a clearer interface with defence and defence needs financial expertise to turn priorities into market-facing propositions, speaking the same language.

Following the autumn budget this year, we will publish the Defence Finance Investment Strategy to set a clear framework for how government and responsible private capital can work together in support of security, resilience and growth. And in December, we will also hold a defence investment summit to turn strategy into delivery and bring together government, industry and investors to accelerate the flow of capital into priority defence capabilities.

Now, before I finish, I want to set out that this is not a theoretical game. This is happening right now and we need to make it easier for it to happen more frequently. In May, 13 British startups were awarded contracts of up to £4 million as part of the Defence Unicorn Fund programme. Kraken Technologies, as one of them, which manufactures maritime uncrewed surface vehicles, has since gone on to raise $175 million in a Series B funding round off the back of a $1 billion valuation. Green Jets is another British firm which has secured significant funding from capital. It was just one of three firms selected by the Ministry of Defence to develop a low-cost drone interceptor. Both Kraken and Green Jets received funding from the National Security Strategic Investment Fund and NATO Innovation Fund, while the British Business Bank also financed Kraken. And JET Connectivity, a small business which builds novel 5G and 6G communications tools was the only British firm to be admitted to the procedures NATO Diana mission track programme earlier this year from over three and a half thousand participants.

That was fantastic recognition of British innovation at its best, but I know it’s just the tip of the iceberg. There are so many other British, brilliant British companies that we need to be able to support as well.

Now, it is in these uncertain times that not only do friends stand together, which is why the support that we offer in Ukraine is long lasting, is serious and will not change no matter what threats Putin throws at us. It is also in these uncertain times that we need to make it easier to bring private capital and public investment together to create the new defence technologies that we need to keep our nation safe.

But let me finish with a final thought. Today we will not only get a clearer view of the potential on offer in the growing defence industry in the UK, and advice on how you can access more of that market. We also get a chance to keep Britain secure in a more dangerous world. Defence needs to be a national endeavour. A whole of society endeavour, a whole of government endeavour. It is the responsibility of the Ministry of Defence to lead that, but it is not the responsibility of the Ministry of Defence alone. To keep our nation safe, we need every part of society, every part of government and industry to step up to support that resilience, that innovation, and that drive to keep us all safe. Because as we can see from our friends in Ukraine, where deterrence fails, not only is it more and more expensive in treasure and lives and lost opportunity. It’s something that, as everyone here, we must take steps to avoid. That is why deterrence matters. That’s why increasing our deterrence matters with new technologies. But if deterrence fails, we must be ready to fight, and we must be ready to win. And all of you in this group can play a part in doing so.

Thank you for what you’re doing here today, and thank you Lady Mayor for bringing us all together.

items.title: Defence support: bullying, harassment or discrimination
items.summary: Guidance for Defence personnel on how to raise concerns about bullying, harassment or discrimination and get support.
items.body:
This guidance is for Armed Forces personnel, civil servants, contractors, and their families and friends.

If you have experienced a sexual offence, visit Defence support: sexual offences .

Defence personnel can find additional guidance on how to recognise and respond to unacceptable or criminal behaviour and access support on the Call it Out hub on Defence Gateway .

If you have experienced unacceptable behaviour including bullying, harassment, sexual harassment or discrimination, support is available.

This page explains how you can raise a complaint and get support.

Unacceptable behaviour has no place in Defence and concerns will be taken seriously.

You may wish to:

seek advice

resolve the issue informally

make a formal complaint

Support is available whatever approach you choose.

If illegal or criminal behaviour has occurred, this should be reported to the Service Police , MOD Police or civilian police as soon as possible.

If you are unsure if what you’ve seen or experienced is unacceptable behaviour, you can read the definition of the behaviours in Behaviours and informal complaints resolution (JSP 763) - GOV.UK .

Raise a complaint

Seek informal resolution

In some circumstances, concerns can be resolved informally. Early action can help stop issues escalating, address misunderstandings and restore working relationships.

Informal resolution does not mean the matter is less important or will not be taken seriously. The main difference is that informal processes are often simpler and can help resolve issues more quickly.

Service or civilian personnel may wish to:

speak directly to the person, if you feel comfortable doing so

seek advice or intervention from a manager or Chain of Command, adviser or another trusted person

use local support, mediation or advisory services available within Defence

You can choose to make a formal complaint at any time.

For more information read Behaviours and informal complaints resolution (JSP 763) .

Defence personnel can also find more detailed information on the Call it Out hub on Defence Gateway .

Service Complaint

Current and former members of the Armed Forces can make a Service Complaint if they believe they have been wronged on a matter that arises under service law.

This can include complaints of bullying, harassment, discrimination and biased, improper or dishonest behaviour.

You can:

complete the Service Complaint Form on the My Complaint app, accessible via Defence Gateway , or:

submit a Service Complaint in writing using the form found at Annex F of JSP 831 Part 2 - GOV.UK

For more information read the guidance on the Armed Forces Service Complaints process - GOV.UK or at Redress of individual grievances: service complaints (JSP 831) - GOV.UK .

Civilian Formal Complaint

Defence civil servants, contractors, consultants and agency workers can raise formal complaints or grievances about bullying, harassment, discrimination or victimisation through the MOD Civilian Formal Complaints Process.

You can use the My Complaints App on Defence Gateway to:

submit a formal complaint

submit an anonymous complaint

record an incident, even if you do not wish to make a complaint at that time

If you cannot access the app, contact the DBS HR Advisory and Casework Service:

civilian personnel enquiry centre: 0800 345 7772 (UK) or +44 1225 747772 (Overseas), 8am to 4pm Monday to Friday

submit a form via the Digital Workplace (DWP)

Email: peopleservices@dbs.mod.uk

Support is available whether or not you choose to make a complaint.

Get support

Support is available whether or not you choose to make a formal complaint. You may want advice, help understanding your options, or simply someone to talk to before deciding what to do next.

You do not need to make a formal complaint to access support. Different services can provide practical advice, emotional support and information about the options available to you.

Available to all personnel:

Local support

If you would prefer to speak to someone directly, support is available through local Defence networks.

You can speak to:

a friend or colleague

your manager or Chain of Command

welfare staff

a diversity and inclusion adviser

staff networks

a padre or chaplain

a Trade Union representative (civilian personnel only) for advice and support on workplace issues and complaints processes.

If you choose to inform your Chain of Command about a sexual offence, their duty of care means they must tell the Service Police.

Bullying, Harassment and Discrimination Helpline

A confidential helpline is available for military personnel, civil servants and contractors.

Trained advisers can provide emotional support, practical advice and guidance on the support available to you. The helpline is open 24/7, 365 days a year and offers a safe, anonymous space to discuss concerns.

Telephone: 0800 014 2381 (UK) or +44 330 008 5942 (Overseas)

Confidential hotline

If you have concerns about wrongdoing, misconduct, illegal activity, safety risks or behaviour that falls below the standards expected in Defence, you can seek confidential advice and guidance for raising a concern and whistleblowing in Defence.

Email: Confidential-hotline@mod.gov.uk

Further information can be found in the MOD Raising a Concern Policy .

Defence Victim and Witness Care Unit

The Defence Victim and Witness Care Unit (VWCU) provide support for victims and witnesses of serious crime committed by people who are under service law in the UK and overseas.

It is independent of the chain of command and you can self-refer.

Victim Liaison Officers (VLOs) can explain what support is available, help you access services and make sure your views are understood.

Helpline: text or call 07974 074259.

Available Monday to Thursday, 8am to 4pm, and Friday, 8am to 3:30pm, excluding bank holidays.

Email: People-DSCC-VWCUGroup@mod.gov.uk

For more information visit the Victim Witness Care Unit GOV.UK page.

Support for Service personnel, veterans and their families:

The Armed Forces Commissioner

The role of the Commissioner is to provide independent and impartial oversight of the Service Complaints system for members of the UK Armed Forces.

It is also to act as a direct point of contact for serving personnel and their families who can raise general service welfare concerns that may impact on their service lives and their ability to serve.

telephone: 0300 369 0689

enquiry form

email: contact@scoaf.org.uk

For more information visit the Armed Forces Commissioner website.

Aurora New Dawn

Aurora New Dawn is a charity that provides free and confidential support for UK Armed Forces personnel and their families, including those deployed overseas. It is independent from Defence and the Chain of Command.

The specialist team can support you if you are experiencing domestic abuse, sexual violence or stalking.

Call the helpline or WhatsApp: +44 (0)333 0912 527

Helpline hours (GMT): 9am to 3pm, Monday to Friday.

WhatsApp service (GMT): Tuesday 9am to 3pm, Wednesday and Thursday 5pm to 8pm, Sunday 10am to 2pm.

For more information visit the Aurora Dawn Armed Forces website.

SSAFA Safe to Serve

SSAFA, the Armed Forces charity, is a source of support for serving personnel, veterans and their families.

SSAFA Safe To Serve is a dedicated support service for women currently serving in HM Armed Forces who are experiencing bullying, discrimination, harassment, or sexual harassment. It is outside the military Chain of Command.

Telephone: Speak directly to an advisor by calling + 44 800 260 6722

Webform: Use the webform to send a message

WhatsApp: Send a message securely on +44 203 807 4400

If you are not a woman currently serving in HM Armed Forces but you would like to speak to SSAFA, please contact SSAFA Forcesline online or telephone +44 800 260 6780 (9am to 5pm Monday to Thursday and 9am to 4pm on Friday).

Veterans UK

Veterans UK provides support and guidance for veterans, former members of the Armed Forces, and their families.

It can provide information on welfare support, compensation schemes, pensions and other services available to the veteran community.

call: 0808 1914 218

For more information visit Veterans UK .

Support for civilians and contractors:

Employee Assistance Programme (EAP)

If you are a civilian, the Employee Assistance Programme (EAP) is a confidential service available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. It can help with personal or work-related issues. EAP will not share any information with your employer or managers.

Helpline:

0800 731 8629 (UK)

+44 330 008 5959 (outside the UK)

contact form

For more information, visit the Workplace wellbeing website.

If you are deployed or based overseas:

If you are overseas, you can access the same support options as in the UK.

Bullying, Harassment, and Discrimination Helpline: +44 330 008 5942

Confidential Hotline for whistleblowing: confidential-hotline@mod.gov.uk

SSAFA Safe to Serve - WhatsApp: +44 203 807 4400

Aurora New Dawn - Helpline and WhatsApp: +44 (0)333 0912 527.

Employee Assistance Programme - +44 330 008 5959

Other support organisations

If you prefer to seek support outside of Defence, specialist organisations can provide information, advice and practical support.

General advice and support

Citizen’s Advice

The Samaritans

Help at Hand

The Charity for Civil Servants

Armed Forces, families and veterans

Naval Families Federation / Army Families Federation / RAF Families Federation

Combat Stress

The Royal British Legion

Bullying, harassment, discrimination and whistleblowing

National Bullying Helpline

Protect

Bullies Out

Acas

Related information

If you have experienced a sexual offence, visit Defence support: sexual offences on GOV.UK.

Defence personnel can find more guidance on how to recognise and respond to unacceptable or criminal behaviour and get support on the Call it Out hub on Defence Gateway .

items.title: Defence support: sexual offences
items.summary: Guidance for Defence personnel on how to report sexual offences and get support at home and overseas.
items.body:
This guidance is for Armed Forces personnel, civil servants, contractors, and their families and friends.

It explains how to:

report a sexual offence

get medical help

get support

You don’t have to make a report at all to receive support.

Report a sexual offence

If you or someone else is in immediate danger in the UK, call 999.

You can report a sexual offence to either the civilian police or the Service Police.

If you are unsure which organisation to contact, either organisation can explain your options and help you access support. You will be listened to without judgement.

It doesn’t matter whether the offence happened recently or in the past.

Civilian police

If you are in immediate danger in the UK, call 999.

If you have a hearing or speech impairment, use the textphone service 18000, or text if you’ve pre-registered with the emergency SMS service .

If you are in danger and you can’t speak or answer questions:

call 999

press 55 when prompted and your call will be transferred to the police

Pressing 55 only works on mobiles and doesn’t allow the police to track your location. If you don’t press 55, your call will be ended.

If it is not an emergency, call 101.

Service Police

The Service Police is responsible for policing armed forces personnel and civilians subject to service discipline.

You can report the incident to the Service Police in the UK or overseas if the incident involves a person who is subject to Service Law or a civilian subject to service discipline.

You can:

call the Service Police Crime Bureau on 02392 285 170 or 0331 145 7630

attend or call a local Service Police station (the Service Police Crime Bureau will be able to provide a location and contact details)

Specially trained officers will provide support, explain your options, and make sure your needs and wishes are considered.

The Defence Serious Crime Command (DSCC) is an independent, professional and global Service Police force with jurisdiction to investigate serious crime committed by those subject to Service law, in the UK and overseas.

Give information anonymously

If you have information about a sexual offence, you can give information anonymously to Crimestoppers.

Call on 0800 555 111

Fill out an anonymous form

If you have experienced a sexual offence and wish to report a crime, you should contact the police directly to get support and advice.

For more information visit the Crimestoppers website.

Get medical help

Medical centre

Your local medical centre or GP practice is a safe place to ask for help.

Medical staff can provide physical and mental healthcare, refer you to specialist services and support your wellbeing at work.

They will not normally share information unless there is a risk of serious harm to you or someone else.

NHS Sexual Assault Referral Centre

A Sexual Assault Referral Centre (SARC) is a specialist NHS service for anyone who has been raped, sexually assaulted or abused.

You can contact a SARC without reporting to the police. You can go at any time, and do not have to go alone.

Find your nearest sexual assault referral centre

SARCs can offer medical, practical and emotional support. They have specially trained doctors, nurses and support workers to care for you.

Services are free and available to everyone regardless of gender, age, the type of incident, or when it happened.

Services include:

crisis care

medical and forensic examination

emergency contraception

sexual health support

access to a sexual assault advisor

referral to mental health support and sexual violence support

For more information visit NHS help after rape and sexual assault .

Get support

You can access support whether or not you choose to make a formal report.

There is no wrong way to seek support.

Different services can provide information, practical help and emotional support, depending on what you need.

Defence personnel can find more guidance on how to recognise and respond to unacceptable or criminal behaviour and get support on the Call it Out hub on Defence Gateway .

Available to all personnel:

Local support

If you would prefer to speak to someone directly, support is available through local Defence networks.

You can speak to:

a friend or colleague

your manager or Chain of Command

welfare staff

a diversity and inclusion adviser

staff networks

a padre or chaplain

a Trade Union representative (civilian personnel only) for advice and support on workplace issues and complaints processes

If you choose to inform your Chain of Command about a sexual offence, their duty of care means they must tell the Service Police.

Defence Victim Witness Care Unit

The Defence Victim Witness Care Unit (VWCU) provide support for victims and witnesses of serious crime committed by people who are under service law in the UK and overseas.

It is independent of the Chain of Command and you can self-refer.

Victim Liaison Officers (VLOs) can explain what support is available, help you access services and make sure your views are understood.

Helpline: text or call 07974 074259.

Available Monday to Thursday, 8am to 4pm, and Friday, 8am to 3:30pm, excluding bank holidays.

Email: People-DSCC-VWCUGroup@mod.gov.uk

For more information visit the Victim Witness Care Unit GOV.UK page.

Independent Legal Advisors scheme

The Independent Legal Advisors (ILA) scheme provides free, independent legal advice and guidance for eligible Service and civilian personnel aged 18 or over, where a reported sexual offence is being investigated within the Service Justice System.

The scheme can help you understand the justice process, your legal rights, what to expect during an investigation, how personal information may be requested or used, and the options available if you are unhappy with how your case has been handled.

The ILA will not tell you what decisions to make or advocate on your behalf. Their role is to give you the information and advice you need to understand your options and make informed choices.

Accessing the scheme is voluntary. Referrals can be made by organisations supporting you, including the Service Police, Defence Serious Crime Command or the Victim Witness Care Unit, and will only be made with your consent.

Support for Service personnel, veterans and their families:

Aurora New Dawn

Aurora New Dawn is a charity that provides free and confidential support for UK Armed Forces personnel and their families, including those deployed overseas. It is independent from Defence and the Chain of Command.

The specialist team can support you if you are experiencing domestic abuse, sexual violence or stalking.

Call the helpline or WhatsApp: +44 (0)333 0912 527

Helpline hours (GMT): 9am to 3pm, Monday to Friday.

WhatsApp service (GMT): Tuesday 9am to 3pm, Wednesday and Thursday 5pm to 8pm, Sunday 10am to 2pm.

For more information visit the Aurora Dawn Armed Forces website.

Veterans UK

Veterans UK provides support and guidance for veterans, former members of the Armed Forces, and their families.

It can provide information on welfare support, compensation schemes, pensions and other services available to the veteran community.

call: 0808 1914 218

For more information visit Veterans UK .

Support for civilians and contractors:

Employee Assistance Programme (EAP)

If you are a civilian, the Employee Assistance Programme (EAP) is a confidential service available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. It can help with personal or work-related issues. EAP will not share any information with your employer or managers.

Helpline:

0800 731 8629 (UK)

+44 330 008 5959 (outside the UK)

contact form

For more information, visit the Workplace wellbeing website.

If you are deployed or based overseas:

If you are deployed or based overseas, support arrangements may be different from those available in the UK.

Contact the local Service Police in the first instance and they can explain the support and services available to you. If local Service Police support is not available, contact the Service Police Crime Bureau on 02392 285 170 or 0331 145 7630 for advice and support.

Defence medical staff can provide advice on the support and care available in your location.

You can also access support from:

Aurora New Dawn - Helpline and WhatsApp: +44 (0)333 0912 527.

Employee Assistance Programme - +44 330 008 5959 (outside the UK)

Victim of rape and sexual assault abroad – GOV.UK

Other support organisations

Victim and witness services - GOV.UK

Victims of crime and sexual violence

Victim Support

Survivors UK

Rape Crisis England and Wales

Support for victims and witnesses of stalking or harassment

Domestic abuse

Women’s Aid

National Centre for Domestic Violence

Men’s Advice Line

Respect

Related information

If you have experienced other unacceptable behaviours which might include being:

bullied

harassed (sexually or otherwise)

discriminated against

victimised after raising a concern

Find more information on GOV.UK: Defence support: bullying, harassment or discrimination .

items.title: Global Strike’s North Star Readiness Campaign bolsters operational readiness
items.author: Capt. Sydney Sedlak
items.summary: Air Force Global Strike Command, in partnership with Air Force Materiel Command and the Defense Logistics Agency, has launched the “North Star Readiness Campaign,” a sweeping initiative aimed at increasing the number of mission-capable B-52 Stratofortress and B-1 Lancer aircraft.
items.body: Air Force Global Strike Command, in partnership with Air Force Materiel Command and the Defense Logistics Agency, has launched the “North Star Readiness Campaign,” a sweeping initiative aimed at increasing the number of mission-capable B-52 Stratofortress and B-1 Lancer aircraft.

items.title: DAF accelerates joint C2 with AI, Space Force integration in latest DASH experiment
items.author: Deb Henley, 505th Command and Control Wing Public Affairs
items.summary: In a fast-paced, two-week experiment, the Department of the Air Force continued to demonstrate that human-machine teaming, integrating artificial intelligence to handle heavy data processing so human operators can make faster and smarter decisions, can significantly accelerate the joint kill chain.

items.title: CSAF, CMSAF highlight forward readiness, deterrence during visit to Spangdahlem Air Base
items.author: Pentagon News
items.summary: Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Ken Wilsbach and Chief Master Sergeant of the Air Force David R. Wolfe visited Spangdahlem Air Base where they met with Airmen and received updates on how the 52nd Fighter Wing is sustaining operations across the European theater.
